comments.text:
Fixed staging/sm/TypedArray/sort_modifications.js by replacing the comparator-provided TypedArray insertion sort with a stable merge sort over the pre-sort storage snapshot. Root cause: the fixture feeds descending arrays up to length 1024 across every TypedArray constructor and uses a comparator with side effects. The previous insertion-sort path was quadratic in comparator calls, so both variants timed out. The new comparator path keeps the existing snapshot-before-sort/write-after-sort semantics, but reduces comparator sorting to O(n log n). The no-comparator path continues through the native/default sort helper added for the counting-sort issue.

Verification:
- Before: cargo run --release -p lyng-js-test262 -- --filter staging/sm/TypedArray/sort_modifications.js --list-failures --report /tmp/lyng-js-typedarray-sort-modifications-before.md -j 1 => timeout after 1s in both variants.
- After: cargo run --release -p lyng-js-test262 -- --filter staging/sm/TypedArray/sort_modifications.js --list-failures --report /tmp/lyng-js-typedarray-sort-modifications-after.md -j 1 => 1/1 files passed, 2/2 variants passed in ~0.2s.

comments.text: Implemented eval global deletion fix. Fix: eval global seeding now defines the configurable properties without adding those names to [[VarNames]], preserving existing script var names for pre-existing globals. Added regression direct_eval_in_global_code_creates_deletable_new_var_binding. title: Burn down Test262 staging failures and skips
description:
Classify and burn down the Test262 `staging/` category for Lyng JS, separating in-scope Stage 3+ ECMA-262 proposal behavior from SpiderMonkey-extension, host-only, or otherwise out-of-scope cases.

Current baseline from `reports/js/lyng-js/test262.md`: `staging` has 1484 selected files, 1477 runnable files, 1298 passed files, 179 failed files, 7 skipped files, and 0 panicked files. Variant totals show 2785 selected variants, 2771 runnable variants, 2462 passed variants, 309 failed variants, and 14 skipped variants. Visible clusters include `staging/sm/RegExp`, `staging/sm/Function`, strict-mode cases, classes/fields, Iterator helpers, TypedArray, RegExp named groups, explicit resource management, Temporal removed-method behavior, and some host-only `IsHTMLDDA` skips.

Relevant areas: `testdata/test262/test/staging/`, `reports/js/lyng-js/test262.md`, `reports/js/lyng-js/test262-exclusions.txt`, `tools/lyng-js-test262/`, and the parser/compiler/vm/builtins/runtime crates touched by each classified cluster.

Create focused child issues for the largest coherent clusters before implementation work so the staging tail does not become one unreviewable grab bag.
acceptance:
A staging classification pass identifies each remaining failure cluster as in-scope implementation work, harness/report work, host-only exclusion, proposal-stage exclusion, or out of scope.
In-scope staging failures are burned down with focused crate-level regression tests and targeted Test262 filtered runs.
A fresh `cargo run --release -p lyng-js-test262 -- --filter staging --report /tmp/lyng-js-staging.md -j 4` run has 0 failed and 0 panicked tests for in-scope staging coverage.
Any remaining skipped or excluded staging tests are backed by explicit manifest entries and documented rationale, not implicit runner behavior.

title: Burn down Test262 staging failures and skips
description:
Classify and burn down the Test262 `staging/` category for Lyng JS, separating in-scope Stage 3+ ECMA-262 proposal behavior from SpiderMonkey-extension, host-only, or otherwise out-of-scope cases.

Current baseline from `reports/js/lyng-js/test262.md`: `staging` has 1484 selected files, 1477 runnable files, 1298 passed files, 179 failed files, 7 skipped files, and 0 panicked files. Variant totals show 2785 selected variants, 2771 runnable variants, 2462 passed variants, 309 failed variants, and 14 skipped variants. Visible clusters include `staging/sm/RegExp`, `staging/sm/Function`, strict-mode cases, classes/fields, Iterator helpers, TypedArray, RegExp named groups, explicit resource management, Temporal removed-method behavior, and some host-only `IsHTMLDDA` skips.

Relevant areas: `testdata/test262/test/staging/`, `reports/js/lyng-js/test262.md`, `reports/js/lyng-js/test262-exclusions.txt`, `tools/lyng-js-test262/`, and the parser/compiler/vm/builtins/runtime crates touched by each classified cluster.

Create focused child issues for the largest coherent clusters before implementation work so the staging tail does not become one unreviewable grab bag.
acceptance:
A staging classification pass identifies each remaining failure cluster as in-scope implementation work, harness/report work, host-only exclusion, proposal-stage exclusion, or out of scope.
In-scope staging failures are burned down with focused crate-level regression tests and targeted Test262 filtered runs.
A fresh `cargo run --release -p lyng-js-test262 -- --filter staging --report /tmp/lyng-js-staging.md -j 4` run has 0 failed and 0 panicked tests for in-scope staging coverage.
Any remaining skipped or excluded staging tests are backed by explicit manifest entries and documented rationale, not implicit runner behavior.

comments.author: 5341456+Feryla@users.noreply.github.com
comments.text: Implemented optional-chain expression fixes. Root causes: runtime-null class heritage was treated like ordinary non-constructor heritage unless the AST was literal null; optional-chain delete returned true without deleting present properties and evaluated continuation keys after a short-circuit; optional chains in new constructor position lacked parser diagnostics; optional call continuations did not share the shorted flag through following ordinary calls. Fixes: runtime null branch in class prototype-chain lowering, optional-delete lowering for hops and continuations, parser diagnostics for optional chains in new constructor position, and shared short-circuit propagation for call continuations. Added focused regressions in optional_chaining and diagnostics coverage. Verification: cargo test -p lyng-js-tests optional_chain -- --nocapture; cargo test -p lyng-js-parser optional -- --nocapture; cargo test -p lyng-js-parser; cargo test -p lyng-js-compiler optional -- --nocapture; cargo test -p lyng-js-compiler; Test262 staging/sm/expressions/optional-chain-class-heritage.js; Test262 staging/sm/expressions/optional-chain.js; Test262 staging/sm/expressions; cargo fmt --all; git diff --check. title: Burn down Test262 staging failures and skips
description:
Classify and burn down the Test262 `staging/` category for Lyng JS, separating in-scope Stage 3+ ECMA-262 proposal behavior from SpiderMonkey-extension, host-only, or otherwise out-of-scope cases.

Current baseline from `reports/js/lyng-js/test262.md`: `staging` has 1484 selected files, 1477 runnable files, 1298 passed files, 179 failed files, 7 skipped files, and 0 panicked files. Variant totals show 2785 selected variants, 2771 runnable variants, 2462 passed variants, 309 failed variants, and 14 skipped variants. Visible clusters include `staging/sm/RegExp`, `staging/sm/Function`, strict-mode cases, classes/fields, Iterator helpers, TypedArray, RegExp named groups, explicit resource management, Temporal removed-method behavior, and some host-only `IsHTMLDDA` skips.

Relevant areas: `testdata/test262/test/staging/`, `reports/js/lyng-js/test262.md`, `reports/js/lyng-js/test262-exclusions.txt`, `tools/lyng-js-test262/`, and the parser/compiler/vm/builtins/runtime crates touched by each classified cluster.

Create focused child issues for the largest coherent clusters before implementation work so the staging tail does not become one unreviewable grab bag.
acceptance:
A staging classification pass identifies each remaining failure cluster as in-scope implementation work, harness/report work, host-only exclusion, proposal-stage exclusion, or out of scope.
In-scope staging failures are burned down with focused crate-level regression tests and targeted Test262 filtered runs.
A fresh `cargo run --release -p lyng-js-test262 -- --filter staging --report /tmp/lyng-js-staging.md -j 4` run has 0 failed and 0 panicked tests for in-scope staging coverage.
Any remaining skipped or excluded staging tests are backed by explicit manifest entries and documented rationale, not implicit runner behavior.

title: Burn down Test262 staging failures and skips
Burn down Test262 staging failures and skips
description:
Classify and burn down the Test262 `staging/` category for Lyng JS, separating in-scope Stage 3+ ECMA-262 proposal behavior from SpiderMonkey-extension, host-only, or otherwise out-of-scope cases.

Current baseline from `reports/js/lyng-js/test262.md`: `staging` has 1484 selected files, 1477 runnable files, 1298 passed files, 179 failed files, 7 skipped files, and 0 panicked files. Variant totals show 2785 selected variants, 2771 runnable variants, 2462 passed variants, 309 failed variants, and 14 skipped variants. Visible clusters include `staging/sm/RegExp`, `staging/sm/Function`, strict-mode cases, classes/fields, Iterator helpers, TypedArray, RegExp named groups, explicit resource management, Temporal removed-method behavior, and some host-only `IsHTMLDDA` skips.

Relevant areas: `testdata/test262/test/staging/`, `reports/js/lyng-js/test262.md`, `reports/js/lyng-js/test262-exclusions.txt`, `tools/lyng-js-test262/`, and the parser/compiler/vm/builtins/runtime crates touched by each classified cluster.

Create focused child issues for the largest coherent clusters before implementation work so the staging tail does not become one unreviewable grab bag.
acceptance:
A staging classification pass identifies each remaining failure cluster as in-scope implementation work, harness/report work, host-only exclusion, proposal-stage exclusion, or out of scope.
In-scope staging failures are burned down with focused crate-level regression tests and targeted Test262 filtered runs.
A fresh `cargo run --release -p lyng-js-test262 -- --filter staging --report /tmp/lyng-js-staging.md -j 4` run has 0 failed and 0 panicked tests for in-scope staging coverage.
Any remaining skipped or excluded staging tests are backed by explicit manifest entries and documented rationale, not implicit runner behavior.

title: Burn down Test262 staging failures and skips
description:
Classify and burn down the Test262 `staging/` category for Lyng JS, separating in-scope Stage 3+ ECMA-262 proposal behavior from SpiderMonkey-extension, host-only, or otherwise out-of-scope cases.

Current baseline from `reports/js/lyng-js/test262.md`: `staging` has 1484 selected files, 1477 runnable files, 1298 passed files, 179 failed files, 7 skipped files, and 0 panicked files. Variant totals show 2785 selected variants, 2771 runnable variants, 2462 passed variants, 309 failed variants, and 14 skipped variants. Visible clusters include `staging/sm/RegExp`, `staging/sm/Function`, strict-mode cases, classes/fields, Iterator helpers, TypedArray, RegExp named groups, explicit resource management, Temporal removed-method behavior, and some host-only `IsHTMLDDA` skips.

Relevant areas: `testdata/test262/test/staging/`, `reports/js/lyng-js/test262.md`, `reports/js/lyng-js/test262-exclusions.txt`, `tools/lyng-js-test262/`, and the parser/compiler/vm/builtins/runtime crates touched by each classified cluster.

Create focused child issues for the largest coherent clusters before implementation work so the staging tail does not become one unreviewable grab bag.
acceptance:
A staging classification pass identifies each remaining failure cluster as in-scope implementation work, harness/report work, host-only exclusion, proposal-stage exclusion, or out of scope.
In-scope staging failures are burned down with focused crate-level regression tests and targeted Test262 filtered runs.
A fresh `cargo run --release -p lyng-js-test262 -- --filter staging --report /tmp/lyng-js-staging.md -j 4` run has 0 failed and 0 panicked tests for in-scope staging coverage.
Any remaining skipped or excluded staging tests are backed by explicit manifest entries and documented rationale, not implicit runner behavior.

notes: Implemented strict assignment lowering for class computed-name and heritage expression evaluation in sloppy outer code. Reproduced staging/sm/class/strictExecution.js before as 0/1 files failed, with only the non-strict variant failing Test262Error in /tmp/lyng-js-class-strict-execution-before.md. title: Burn down Test262 staging failures and skips
Make shared backing stores cross-agent ready and reduce typed-array access overhead
description: Review finding: AgentCluster and cluster handles use Rc<RefCell<BackingStoreRuntime>> and Rc<RefCell<SharedMemoryRuntime>>, while shared backing-store bytes use Arc<Mutex<Vec<u8>>>. Typed-array storage helpers read and write byte by byte through backing_store_get_byte and backing_store_set_byte, causing repeated RefCell borrows and mutex locks for multi-byte elements. This conflicts with the architecture for cluster-owned cross-agent coordination and narrow typed atomic access. Relevant files: crates/lyng-js/env/src/cluster.rs, crates/lyng-js/env/src/agent/cluster_handles.rs, crates/lyng-js/env/src/backing_store.rs, crates/lyng-js/builtins/src/public/dispatch/binary_data/typed_arrays.rs.
acceptance: Shared backing-store ownership is suitable for the intended cross-agent host boundary or the remaining single-thread limitation is explicitly documented and tracked. Typed-array read/write helpers use element-width or slice-level access instead of byte-at-a-time public calls in hot paths. Atomics use a narrow typed access boundary with alignment and bounds checks above it. Add focused benchmarks or report rows for typed-array read/write/fill/copy and Atomics operations before and after.

Use hash-backed weak collection storage
description: Latest full Test262 report after earlier optimizations is still 105.3s. The slowest file is testdata/test262/test/staging/sm/regress/regress-1507322-deep-weakmap.js at ~14.1s total in the full report and ~6.9s for two variants with -j 2. A process sample of the worker for that file (/tmp/lyng-js-weakmap-worker.sample.txt) showed 1608/2258 samples in lyng_js_gc::weak::WeakMapState::get and 606/2258 samples in PrimitiveHeap::weak_map_set. Current implementation in crates/lyng-js/gc/src/weak.rs stores WeakMapState entries in a Vec, so a 100k-entry chain turns WeakMap.prototype.get/set into linear scans. Improve interpreter-level Test262 performance by making weak map lookups and updates sublinear while preserving weak collection semantics, GC sweeping, snapshots, and existing public behavior.
acceptance: WeakMap get/set/delete semantics remain covered by focused tests; regress-1507322-deep-weakmap.js targeted Test262 slice is materially faster than the ~6.9s two-variant baseline; full report is rerun or a fresh next-hotspot report is produced before setting in_review.

Fast-path primitive number binary opcodes
description: Full Test262 report remains ~106s after weak-map optimization. Current slowest files include decodeURI/decodeURIComponent (~8.4s each) and toSpliced (~13.5s). Samples for decodeURI show the actual decodeURI builtin is not dominant; time is mostly in VM dispatch plus JS helper arithmetic/string construction. crates/lyng-js/vm/src/vm/dispatch.rs already has try_smi_binary_opcode, but it only returns Some for two Smi operands. Helpers such as decimalToPercentHexString produce primitive doubles through modulo/division and then route through generic ToPrimitive/ToNumeric paths for arithmetic/comparison. Acceptance: add an interpreter-level primitive-number fast path for double/mixed numeric operands without bypassing object/string/bigint semantics; verify focused VM tests and relevant Test262 URI slice; update this issue with before/after timings.

Avoid temporary buffers for UTF-16 string concat
description: The RegExp property-escapes generated Test262 profile at /tmp/lyng-js-regexp-property-generated.sample.txt shows a large string-building cost under Vm::add_values -> concat_string_refs, with PrimitiveHeap::alloc_string, memmove, and SideAllocator reserve/copy visible while testdata/test262/harness/regExpUtils.js buildString repeatedly appends String.fromCodePoint chunks. Latin-1 direct concat already avoids the temporary Vec path, but UTF-16 and mixed Latin-1/UTF-16 concatenation still materialize a temporary byte Vec before allocating and copying into side storage. description: Review finding: AgentCluster and cluster handles use Rc<RefCell<BackingStoreRuntime>> and Rc<RefCell<SharedMemoryRuntime>>, while shared backing-store bytes use Arc<Mutex<Vec<u8>>>. Relevant files: crates/lyng-js/env/src/cluster.rs, crates/lyng-js/env/src/agent/cluster_handles.rs, crates/lyng-js/env/src/backing_store.rs, crates/lyng-js/builtins/src/public/dispatch/binary_data/typed_arrays.rs.
acceptance: Shared backing-store ownership is suitable for the intended cross-agent host boundary or the remaining single-thread limitation is explicitly documented and tracked. Typed-array read/write helpers use element-width or slice-level access instead of byte-at-a-time public calls in hot paths. Atomics use a narrow typed access boundary with alignment and bounds checks above it. title: Restore the Lyng JS pedantic/nursery Clippy gate
description: Review finding: the documented gate cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -W clippy::pedantic -W clippy::nursery completed but reported thousands of warnings. High-volume categories included Option::map_or_else suggestions, missing const fn opportunities, raw string hash simplifications, collapsible ifs, missing errors docs, wildcard imports, and related pedantic/nursery findings.
acceptance: All Lyng JS crates and tools pass the documented Clippy command without broad new allow attributes. Intentional lint suppressions are narrow, local, and justified. The final issue notes record the exact command output and any remaining documented exceptions.

Fixed the Date.UTC Test262 report regression that appeared while regenerating the whole report. Root cause: the Clippy cleanup had replaced Date MakeTime/MakeDate arithmetic with fused mul_add, but ECMA-262 requires ordinary Number multiplication and addition order there. The runtime now uses explicit arithmetic with narrow local suboptimal_flops justifications, and script_core_date_utc_uses_ecmascript_floating_point_operation_order covers the two Test262 cases.

description: Review finding after all existing lyng-4umq children were closed: active Lyng JS public surfaces still expose phase-era scaffold/placeholder APIs. This conflicts with the epic acceptance criterion that active code no longer exposes phase-era placeholder APIs and with the live-engine wording in docs/lyng-js.
acceptance: Remove or make private/test-only the public marker and installable_* scaffold APIs unless each has a real non-placeholder architecture role documented in docs/lyng-js. Audit broad Clippy allow lists in Lyng JS crate roots
description: Review finding: the Clippy gate is quiet for Lyng JS partly because many crate roots still use broad crate-level allow lists without local rationale. Evidence includes crates/lyng-js/compiler/src/lib.rs, builtins/src/lib.rs, vm/src/lib.rs, common/src/lib.rs, gc/src/lib.rs, env/src/lib.rs, ast/src/lib.rs, bytecode/src/lib.rs, types/src/lib.rs, ops/src/lib.rs, objects/src/lib.rs, parser/src/lib.rs, lexer/src/lib.rs, cli/src/lib.rs, and sema/src/lib.rs. Common examples suppress clippy::module_name_repetitions, clippy::must_use_candidate, clippy::return_self_not_must_use, clippy::cast_possible_truncation, clippy::redundant_closure_for_method_calls, or similar across an entire crate. docs/lyng-js/engineering-standards.md says lint suppressions should be deliberate, locally justified, and treated as design feedback, so these broad root allows reduce the value of the restored gate.
acceptance: For each Lyng JS crate-level Clippy allow, either remove it, narrow it to the smallest module/function/type, or replace it with a documented allow/expect reason that explains the deliberate API or hot-path tradeoff. Keep test-only broad allowances separated from production code. After the audit, rg "^#!\\[allow\\(" crates/lyng-js should show only justified crate-level policies or test-only exceptions. Run cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -W clippy::pedantic -W clippy::nursery and the focused tests for touched crates.

acceptance: Move module graph loading/linking/evaluation/export resolution/namespace-object logic out of crates/lyng-js/vm/src/vm.rs into focused VM child modules with clear ownership. Remove stale "until the VM module split issue extracts it" reason strings. Preserve behavior with cargo test -p lyng-js-vm, cargo test -p lyng-js-tests, and a relevant module/dynamic-import Test262 slice if module behavior changes.

Audit broad Clippy allow lists in Lyng JS crate roots
description: Review finding: the Clippy gate is quiet for Lyng JS partly because many crate roots still use broad crate-level allow lists without local rationale. Evidence includes crates/lyng-js/compiler/src/lib.rs, builtins/src/lib.rs, vm/src/lib.rs, common/src/lib.rs, gc/src/lib.rs, env/src/lib.rs, ast/src/lib.rs, bytecode/src/lib.rs, types/src/lib.rs, ops/src/lib.rs, objects/src/lib.rs, parser/src/lib.rs, lexer/src/lib.rs, cli/src/lib.rs, and sema/src/lib.rs. Common examples suppress clippy::module_name_repetitions, clippy::must_use_candidate, clippy::return_self_not_must_use, clippy::cast_possible_truncation, clippy::redundant_closure_for_method_calls, or similar across an entire crate. docs/lyng-js/engineering-standards.md says lint suppressions should be deliberate, locally justified, and treated as design feedback, so these broad root allows reduce the value of the restored gate.
acceptance: For each Lyng JS crate-level Clippy allow, either remove it, narrow it to the smallest module/function/type, or replace it with a documented allow/expect reason that explains the deliberate API or hot-path tradeoff. Keep test-only broad allowances separated from production code. After the audit, rg "^#!\\[allow\\(" crates/lyng-js should show only justified crate-level policies or test-only exceptions. Run cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -W clippy::pedantic -W clippy::nursery and the focused tests for touched crates.

title: Bring Lyng JS code quality up to engine standards
Establish Lyng JS performance engineering loop
description:
Create the main Lyng JS performance engineering track now that runnable ECMA-262/Test262 conformance is green enough to shift focus from correctness coverage toward throughput, memory behavior, and fast bottleneck iteration. This epic is separate from the JIT-tiering epic lyng-5eqw: JIT readiness remains relevant, but the first performance phase should use Test262 and existing in-repo benchmark tooling to expose interpreter/runtime bottlenecks before native-code work becomes the main path.

Current context as of 2026-05-09:
- Whole-suite Test262 report reports 49,706 runnable files passed, 0 failed, 0 panicked, and 69.7s wall time.
- Slowest Test262 files currently include staging/sm/Array/toSpliced-dense.js, decodeURI/decodeURIComponent stress tests, TypedArray sorting/conversion tests, String case mapping, RegExp property escape generated tests, and staging/sm/Date/dst-offset-caching-* tests.
- tools/lyng-js-bench already has runtime, density, and test262 diagnostic modes. The test262 mode emits Markdown plus JSON with phase timings, code-shape metrics, feedback/tiering diagnostics, runtime live-byte deltas, cause hints, and report-only deltas.
- Quick performance triage of staging/sm/Date/dst-offset-caching-2-of-8 showed evaluation-dominated variants with large feedback-vector surfaces and megamorphic inline-cache activity.

Initial direction:
- Use Test262 as the first iteration corpus because it is already integrated, semantically meaningful, and exposes current slow paths.
- Improve tooling so agents can run fast smoke loops, targeted sampled loops, baseline comparisons, and profiler-friendly workloads.
- Use findings to prioritize interpreter/runtime, builtins, object/IC, allocation, metadata, and memory-accounting fixes.
- Add V8/Octane-style benchmark integration as a later child task after the Test262-driven loop is stable.

Out of scope for the epic itself:
- Shipping native-code execution as the default performance strategy.
- Adding heavyweight benchmark dependencies without a separate dependency-policy decision.
- Rewriting core Value, object, frame, bytecode, or GC architecture without a focused child issue.
acceptance:
Epic has child issues covering Test262 performance workflow, benchmark presets/baseline diffing, phase timing/profiler hooks, VM-owned memory accounting, top Test262 bottleneck fixes, and later V8/Octane-style benchmark integration.
The epic links or references existing related issues such as lyng-4uvi, lyng-62fh, and lyng-5eqw where appropriate without conflating interpreter/runtime performance work with the JIT-readiness epic.
The first implementation phase can run in short local loops and produce machine-readable reports that identify bottlenecks and regressions.
No issue is marked in_progress merely because the epic is created.

The output should make it obvious which command to run for smoke triage, targeted resampling, baseline comparison, and handoff to implementation.

Documentation includes macOS sample/xctrace examples and a fallback plain timing loop.
The profiler path does not affect normal benchmark results unless explicitly enabled.

title: Define Test262 performance iteration workflow
Add profiler-friendly Test262 and benchmark targets
description:
Add tooling support for running discovered slow cases under platform profilers and lightweight engine counters. The macOS development environment has sample, xctrace, and dtrace available, while cargo-flamegraph/hyperfine/samply are not assumed. The goal is not to vendor a profiler, but to make it easy to run one stable workload long enough to capture call stacks and correlate them with VM/builtin counters.

Relevant paths: tools/lyng-js-bench, tools/lyng-js-test262, docs/lyng-js or docs/superpowers specs, reports/js/lyng-js/.
acceptance:
A profiler-target command or documented preset repeatedly runs one selected Test262 variant or benchmark workload long enough for sample/xctrace capture.
The target can optionally print opcode counts, builtin call counts, allocation counts, IC state summaries, and slow-path counters if those counters are available without changing guest behavior.
Documentation includes macOS sample/xctrace examples and a fallback plain timing loop.
The profiler path does not affect normal benchmark results unless explicitly enabled.

title: Add profiler-friendly Test262 and benchmark targets

description:
Research and plan a second-phase benchmark corpus using V8/Octane-style performance tests after the Test262-driven performance workflow is stable. The plan should avoid pulling in a large or stale corpus blindly and should define how external benchmarks map to Lyng JS current ECMA-262 scope, missing non-standard APIs, harness requirements, and report format.

This task should not block the first Test262 performance iteration.
acceptance:
Recommendation identifies which V8/Octane-style suites or subsets are appropriate, what licensing/dependency constraints apply, and what harness work is required.
Plan distinguishes strict ECMA-262 workloads from benchmarks requiring browser, Node, Intl, or non-standard APIs.
Report format aligns with lyng-js-bench JSON/Markdown conventions.
No external corpus is vendored or added as a default dependency without a separate approved implementation issue.

title: Plan V8 and Octane benchmark integration after Test262 loop
Split Test262 performance timings into actionable phases
description:
Make Test262 performance diagnostics identify bottlenecks below the current broad evaluation bucket. The current diagnostic flow reports read_source, runtime_assembly, frontend_check, parse, sema, lowering, install_or_load, evaluation, and total. For runtime work, install_or_load/evaluation currently conflate bootstrap, extension installation, global instantiation, execution, and job checkpointing enough that agents still need manual source tracing before choosing a subsystem.

Relevant paths: tools/lyng-js-test262/src/execution.rs, tools/lyng-js-bench/src/test262.rs, crates/lyng-js/vm/src/vm.rs.
acceptance:
Test262 diagnostic output separates at least script install, realm bootstrap, extension installation, global instantiation, bytecode execution, and job checkpoint time where the VM API can expose them cleanly.
Markdown and JSON reports show the refined dominant phase and preserve backward-compatible top-level totals.
A targeted Date DST-offset perf run identifies whether time is spent in execution proper versus setup phases.
Focused tests cover phase aggregation and report rendering.

title: Add benchmark presets and baseline diffing

description:
Run the first Test262-driven performance triage pass and break the top bottlenecks into focused implementation issues. Initial whole-suite evidence points at staging/sm/Array/toSpliced-dense.js, decodeURI/decodeURIComponent stress tests, staging/sm/TypedArray sorting/conversion tests, staging/sm/String/string-upper-lower-mapping.js, generated RegExp property-escape tests, and staging/sm/Date/dst-offset-caching-* tests. Existing Date DST issue lyng-4uvi should be treated as one concrete child/related bottleneck.

This task is for triage and issue breakdown, not for batching unrelated fixes into one change.
acceptance:

Each selected bottleneck has a focused child issue or related issue with owning subsystem, suspected hot path, acceptance criteria, and verification command.
Existing issue lyng-4uvi is linked or updated with current Test262 perf evidence before implementation begins.
No broad interpreter, builtin, or object rewrite is started from this task without a focused issue.

comments.text:

title: Split Test262 performance timings into actionable phases
Add profiler-friendly Test262 and benchmark targets
description:
Add tooling support for running discovered slow cases under platform profilers and lightweight engine counters. The macOS development environment has sample, xctrace, and dtrace available, while cargo-flamegraph/hyperfine/samply are not assumed. The goal is not to vendor a profiler, but to make it easy to run one stable workload long enough to capture call stacks and correlate them with VM/builtin counters.

Relevant paths: tools/lyng-js-bench, tools/lyng-js-test262, docs/lyng-js or docs/superpowers specs, reports/js/lyng-js/.
acceptance:
A profiler-target command or documented preset repeatedly runs one selected Test262 variant or benchmark workload long enough for sample/xctrace capture.
The target can optionally print opcode counts, builtin call counts, allocation counts, IC state summaries, and slow-path counters if those counters are available without changing guest behavior.
Documentation includes macOS sample/xctrace examples and a fallback plain timing loop.
The profiler path does not affect normal benchmark results unless explicitly enabled.

Implementation evidence from 2026-05-09:

Root cause investigation:
- Reproduced the target with target/release/lyng-js-bench test262 --preset smoke --filter staging/sm/String/string-upper-lower-mapping --report /tmp/lyng-js-test262-me3x-baseline.md --json /tmp/lyng-js-test262-me3x-baseline.json --timeout-ms 10000 -j 1 --print-counters.
- Baseline output: slowest median 1012.508ms, dominant_phase=script_install, script_install_ms=731.902, bytecode_execution_ms=194.104, instruction_words=459450, constants=65705, source_map_entries=65602, safepoints=65602, deopt_snapshots=65602, wide_operands=65463.
- Profile target plus macOS sample wrote /tmp/lyng-js-test262-me3x-profile.md, /tmp/lyng-js-test262-me3x-profile.json, and /tmp/lyng-js-test262-me3x.sample.txt. Sampling showed VM install_functions dominating the profile loop.

Changes made:
- Replaced per-constant linear lookup through atom_texts during VM constant installation with an atom-id indexed compiled atom table built alongside canonical_atoms.
- Avoided instruction-length cold metadata side tables for source maps/safepoints/deopt snapshots, preserving lookups through the immutable template; empty direct-eval and loop-iteration offset tables no longer scale to full instruction count.
- Consumed prepared installed templates with take() in the second install pass instead of cloning the BytecodeFunction again.
- Added vm::install::tests::sparse_cold_metadata_indexes_do_not_scale_with_instruction_count to guard the cold metadata footprint and lookup behavior.

Command: target/release/lyng-js-bench test262 --preset smoke --filter built-ins/decodeURI/S15.1.3.1_A2.5_T1 --report /tmp/lyng-js-test262-5br7-decodeuri.md --json /tmp/lyng-js-test262-5br7-decodeuri.json --timeout-ms 10000 -j 1. Result: strict median_total_ms=3673.515, dominant_phase=bytecode_execution, bytecode_execution_ms=3593.188; non-strict median_total_ms=3639.113, bytecode_execution_ms=3562.006. Similar command for decodeURIComponent wrote /tmp/lyng-js-test262-5br7-decodeuricomponent.md and .json; strict median_total_ms=3618.309, bytecode_execution_ms=3539.508. Diagnostics: function_count=19, instruction_words=1248-1249, feedback_slots=416, live_feedback_sites=416, megamorphic_sites=0, runtime_live_bytes_delta about 164MB. Suspected owner: URI builtin dispatch in crates/lyng-js/builtins/src/public/dispatch/language.rs, especially decode_uri_units and repeated string/unit conversion during large exhaustive tests.
acceptance: Representative decodeURI and decodeURIComponent Test262 filters pass and show material median_total_ms/bytecode_execution_ms improvement against the /tmp/lyng-js-test262-5br7-decodeuri*.json baselines. Preserve URIError behavior and decodeURI reserved-escape semantics. Run cargo test coverage for URI builtins plus targeted lyng-js-bench test262 commands for both decodeURI and decodeURIComponent.

comments.author: codex
comments.text: Implemented a stronger URI stress-path optimization after follow-up profiling. Beyond the original decode scratch/direct-dispatch changes, added a bounded Agent cache for repeated short Latin-1 primitive strings so Test262 decimalToPercentHexString-style %XX concatenations avoid repeated payload allocation, and a one-entry two-code-unit cache so decodeURI*/String.fromCharCode surrogate-pair comparisons reuse the same primitive string handle. Added an exact RFC 3629 four-byte percent-sequence fast path for Latin-1 inputs while preserving URIError checks and decodeURI reserved escape behavior. Latest smoke benchmark results: decodeURIComponent S15.1.3.2_A2.5_T1 non-strict 3368.114 ms total / 3335.131 ms bytecode / 73,528,156 live-byte delta; strict 3356.688 ms / 3325.446 ms / 73,528,202. decodeURI S15.1.3.1_A2.5_T1 non-strict 3360.503 ms / 3328.244 ms / 73,528,147; strict 3369.448 ms / 3338.941 ms / 73,528,193. This improves materially over the first pass (~132.6 MB live-byte delta, ~3.45s total) and the original baseline (~164 MB, ~3.6s total). Verified cargo test -p lyng-js-builtins, cargo test -p lyng-js-vm, targeted lyng-js-tests URI cases, cargo clippy on env/builtins/vm with pedantic+nursery, release bench slices, and git diff --check.

comments.author: codex
comments.text: Follow-up after reviewing the 132.6 MB live-byte delta: yes, the first pass was still copying/allocating more than needed, mostly outside the URI decoder. Test262 decimalToPercentHexString builds repeated short Latin-1 strings such as %8F through normal string concatenation, so I added a bounded Agent cache for repeated two- and three-byte Latin-1 primitive strings, routed VM concat and string allocation through it, and kept the two-code-unit surrogate-pair cache plus exact four-byte percent-sequence fast path. Latest smoke benchmark results: decodeURIComponent S15.1.3.2_A2.5_T1 non-strict 3368.114 ms total / 3335.131 ms bytecode / 73,528,156 live-byte delta; strict 3356.688 ms / 3325.446 ms / 73,528,202. decodeURI S15.1.3.1_A2.5_T1 non-strict 3360.503 ms / 3328.244 ms / 73,528,147; strict 3369.448 ms / 3338.941 ms / 73,528,193. This is materially better than the first pass (~132.6 MB, ~3.45s) and the original baseline (~164 MB, ~3.6s). Verification now includes cargo test -p lyng-js-builtins, cargo test -p lyng-js-vm, targeted lyng-js-tests URI cases, cargo clippy on env/builtins/vm with pedantic+nursery, release bench slices, cargo fmt --all, and git diff --check.

title: Set up QuickJS and Boa performance comparison loop
Establish Lyng JS performance engineering loop
description:
Create the main Lyng JS performance engineering track now that runnable ECMA-262/Test262 conformance is green enough to shift focus from correctness coverage toward throughput, memory behavior, and fast bottleneck iteration. This epic is separate from the JIT-tiering epic lyng-5eqw: JIT readiness remains relevant, but the first performance phase should use Test262 and existing in-repo benchmark tooling to expose interpreter/runtime bottlenecks before native-code work becomes the main path.

Current context as of 2026-05-09:
- Whole-suite Test262 report reports 49,706 runnable files passed, 0 failed, 0 panicked, and 69.7s wall time.
- Slowest Test262 files currently include staging/sm/Array/toSpliced-dense.js, decodeURI/decodeURIComponent stress tests, TypedArray sorting/conversion tests, String case mapping, RegExp property escape generated tests, and staging/sm/Date/dst-offset-caching-* tests.
- tools/lyng-js-bench already has runtime, density, and test262 diagnostic modes. The test262 mode emits Markdown plus JSON with phase timings, code-shape metrics, feedback/tiering diagnostics, runtime live-byte deltas, cause hints, and report-only deltas.
- Quick performance triage of staging/sm/Date/dst-offset-caching-2-of-8 showed evaluation-dominated variants with large feedback-vector surfaces and megamorphic inline-cache activity.

Initial direction:
- Use Test262 as the first iteration corpus because it is already integrated, semantically meaningful, and exposes current slow paths.
- Improve tooling so agents can run fast smoke loops, targeted sampled loops, baseline comparisons, and profiler-friendly workloads.
- Use findings to prioritize interpreter/runtime, builtins, object/IC, allocation, metadata, and memory-accounting fixes.
- Add V8/Octane-style benchmark integration as a later child task after the Test262-driven loop is stable.

Out of scope for the epic itself:
- Shipping native-code execution as the default performance strategy.
- Adding heavyweight benchmark dependencies without a separate dependency-policy decision.
- Rewriting core Value, object, frame, bytecode, or GC architecture without a focused child issue.
acceptance:
Epic has child issues covering Test262 performance workflow, benchmark presets/baseline diffing, phase timing/profiler hooks, VM-owned memory accounting, top Test262 bottleneck fixes, and later V8/Octane-style benchmark integration.
The epic links or references existing related issues such as lyng-4uvi, lyng-62fh, and lyng-5eqw where appropriate without conflating interpreter/runtime performance work with the JIT-readiness epic.
The first implementation phase can run in short local loops and produce machine-readable reports that identify bottlenecks and regressions.
No issue is marked in_progress merely because the epic is created.

title: Plan V8 and Octane benchmark integration after Test262 loop
Plan V8 and Octane benchmark integration after Test262 loop
description:
Research and plan a second-phase benchmark corpus using V8/Octane-style performance tests after the Test262-driven performance workflow is stable. This task should not block the first Test262 performance iteration.

No external corpus is vendored or added as a default dependency without a separate approved implementation issue.

description: V8 v7 Crypto is the largest measured Lyng-vs-QuickJS score gap from the 2026-05-10 triage. Establish Lyng JS performance engineering loop
description:
Create the main Lyng JS performance engineering track now that runnable ECMA-262/Test262 conformance is green enough to shift focus from correctness coverage toward throughput, memory behavior, and fast bottleneck iteration. This epic is separate from the JIT-tiering epic lyng-5eqw: JIT readiness remains relevant, but the first performance phase should use Test262 and existing in-repo benchmark tooling to expose interpreter/runtime bottlenecks before native-code work becomes the main path.

Current context as of 2026-05-09:
- Whole-suite Test262 report reports 49,706 runnable files passed, 0 failed, 0 panicked, and 69.7s wall time.
- Slowest Test262 files currently include staging/sm/Array/toSpliced-dense.js, decodeURI/decodeURIComponent stress tests, TypedArray sorting/conversion tests, String case mapping, RegExp property escape generated tests, and staging/sm/Date/dst-offset-caching-* tests.
- tools/lyng-js-bench already has runtime, density, and test262 diagnostic modes. The test262 mode emits Markdown plus JSON with phase timings, code-shape metrics, feedback/tiering diagnostics, runtime live-byte deltas, cause hints, and report-only deltas.
- Quick performance triage of staging/sm/Date/dst-offset-caching-2-of-8 showed evaluation-dominated variants with large feedback-vector surfaces and megamorphic inline-cache activity.

Initial direction:
- Use Test262 as the first iteration corpus because it is already integrated, semantically meaningful, and exposes current slow paths.
- Improve tooling so agents can run fast smoke loops, targeted sampled loops, baseline comparisons, and profiler-friendly workloads.
- Use findings to prioritize interpreter/runtime, builtins, object/IC, allocation, metadata, and memory-accounting fixes.
- Add V8/Octane-style benchmark integration as a later child task after the Test262-driven loop is stable.

Out of scope for the epic itself:
- Shipping native-code execution as the default performance strategy.
- Adding heavyweight benchmark dependencies without a separate dependency-policy decision.
- Rewriting core Value, object, frame, bytecode, or GC architecture without a focused child issue.
acceptance:
Epic has child issues covering Test262 performance workflow, benchmark presets/baseline diffing, phase timing/profiler hooks, VM-owned memory accounting, top Test262 bottleneck fixes, and later V8/Octane-style benchmark integration.
The epic links or references existing related issues such as lyng-4uvi, lyng-62fh, and lyng-5eqw where appropriate without conflating interpreter/runtime performance work with the JIT-readiness epic.
The first implementation phase can run in short local loops and produce machine-readable reports that identify bottlenecks and regressions.
No issue is marked in_progress merely because the epic is created.

comments.author: 5341456+Feryla@users.noreply.github.com
comments.text: Implemented focused Richards/DeltaBlue VM hot-path improvements. Profile evidence: Richards sample at /tmp/lyng-js-cq2w-richards-before.sample.txt showed named property IC state copies/memmove under store hits; DeltaBlue sample at /tmp/lyng-js-cq2w-deltablue-after-first.sample.txt showed Function.prototype.call/call_to_completion and Array.prototype.push overhead. Boa still crashes in this local environment before producing scores. Verification passed: cargo test -p lyng-js-builtins; cargo test -p lyng-js-vm; cargo clippy -p lyng-js-builtins -p lyng-js-vm --all-targets -- -W clippy::pedantic -W clippy::nursery; targeted function_call_builtin and array_push_preserves_index_setter_observability tests after final lint fixes.

A direct table or generated family map can reduce overhead for builtin-heavy string, regexp, URI, array, and Temporal paths while keeping builtins organized by domain.

Reduce call-frame hot-path size and register-stack resize churn
description: The review flags VM call-entry overhead from large frame records and register-stack resizing. Current VM code keeps FrameRecord values in the VM frame stack and finish_frame truncates register_stack on return, while call entry grows the same Vec for each activation. For call-heavy workloads, the hot path should push a compact frame header and use a cursor or preallocated register window where that is simpler and measurable.
acceptance: Measure a call-heavy workload before changing frame layout. Identify which FrameRecord fields are needed per dispatch versus only for exceptions, generators, environments, or debugging. Prototype a compact hot frame header or register-stack cursor without weakening rooting, unwinding, for-in/iterator state cleanup, or mapped-arguments finalization. Verify with cargo test -p lyng-js-vm and a call-heavy benchmark, recording memory and runtime deltas.

Eliminate validated VM register access bounds checks on hot path
description: The review identifies per-access register bounds checks in crates/lyng-js/vm/src/vm/registers.rs. Current read_register and write_register compute an absolute register and perform checked Vec access for every VM register read/write. Because bytecode is compiler-produced and frame register windows are known, the hot interpreter path should validate frame/register invariants once and use a narrow checked-debug or unchecked-release accessor inside dispatch.
acceptance: Define the bytecode/frame invariants that make unchecked hot-path register access sound. Add debug assertions or a validation pass that catches bad register indices during development. Replace hot read/write paths with narrowed register-window access while preserving existing VmError behavior for invalid external or corrupted bytecode paths. Verify with cargo test -p lyng-js-vm and a release benchmark on arithmetic-loop and array-object-loop, recording results.

Vm now exposes VmDispatchMode with the default match loop plus FunctionTable mode, selectable programmatically or with LYNG_JS_VM_DISPATCH=function-table. Baseline before dispatch changes: /tmp/lyng-js-2hhp-baseline-arithmetic.md arithmetic-loop Lyng 11.902ms, QuickJS 6.545ms, Boa failed in system-configuration init; Test262 language/statements/for inner-loop baseline /tmp/lyng-js-2hhp-baseline-test262-for.md slowest median 39.340ms, bytecode_execution dominated. comments.author: codex
comments.text:
Implemented the IC cliff relaxation with TDD coverage. Red evidence before the change: six-shape named and keyed property IC tests both fell to Megamorphic with zero entries, and the feedback snapshot expected Polymorphic but observed Megamorphic.

Changes: raised the polymorphic property cache capacity from 4 to 8, kept promotion to Megamorphic beyond capacity with a 10-shape regression test, and added receiver-shape prefiltering before full cache validation so extra polymorphic entries do not force expensive validation on nonmatching shapes. Matching entries still go through the existing named/keyed cache validation path, preserving stale-shape and invalidation checks. Added a synthetic polymorphic-property-loop benchmark plus synthetic --filter support for compare workloads.

Benchmark evidence: before capacity change, polymorphic-property-loop smoke compare reported lyng-js median 13.167ms / 1.91x quickjs; after the capacity increase plus shape prefilter, it reported 13.261ms / 1.91x quickjs. Boa comparison still fails locally in the existing system-configuration startup path.

title: Fix regenerated Test262 regressions
JIT-ready GC plumbing foundation
description:
Refactor allocation and heap-reference write paths so a future generational collector can be added without invasive call-site changes. This epic is behavior-preserving foundation work for the JIT-ready plan: audit allocation/write sites, introduce a mutator write chokepoint, and reserve generation metadata before nursery work starts.

Why: machine-code allocation and incremental collection require every heap-reference write into heap-resident records to pass through a single barrier-capable API. Missing this foundation risks unsound old-to-young references and marker drift once nursery or incremental GC work begins.

Out of scope: nursery allocation, card marking, incremental marking, concurrent sweep, or native-code/JIT emission.
acceptance:
Child issues cover A1 audit, A2 HeapWriter chokepoint, and A3 generation metadata.
No child issue changes JavaScript observable behavior unless explicitly called out.
The epic remains open and no work is marked in_progress during issue creation.

JIT-ready incremental marking
description:
Split major old-generation marking into bounded mutator-interleaved slices with the write barriers and final stop-the-world finish needed for correctness.

Why: once JIT-tier metadata, feedback entries, deopt records, and OSR frames exist, unbounded stop-the-world mark phases become the wrong latency default. The JIT-ready interpreter needs a precise, enforced collector lifecycle before machine-code execution arrives.

Out of scope: a concurrent marker thread, old-generation compaction, native-code/JIT emission, and changing nursery policy except where required by marker barriers.

Child issues cover C1 mark slicing, C2 Dijkstra-style incremental marking write barrier, and C3 atomic mark-phase finish.
Major-GC pause distributions are reported by the end of the epic.
Test262 pass rate remains unchanged for completed behavior-changing children.

JIT-ready feedback fidelity
description:
Make Lyng JS runtime feedback record the callee and constructor identity information a future JIT needs, without introducing native-code execution.

Why: current call and construct feedback records arity but not target identity. A future JIT would otherwise have to rediscover call-site stability instead of reusing interpreter feedback, weakening tiering decisions and builtin fast paths.

Out of scope: optimizer IR, machine-code generation, broad inline-cache rewrites outside call/construct fidelity, and unsafe benchmark-specific shortcuts.

Bench reports expose call/construct cache states.
Completed children preserve Test262 pass rate and meet their benchmark regression thresholds.

JIT-ready generational nursery
description:
Introduce a bump-allocated nursery for short-lived Lyng JS heap records, promote survivors, and add the remembered-set machinery needed for efficient minor collections.

Why: a future baseline JIT needs cheap allocation paths that share the interpreter collector rather than inventing a separate allocation model. Today Lyng JS allocates directly into longer-lived arenas, so short-lived allocation pressure remains expensive and old-generation scanning would dominate minor GC without barriers.

Out of scope: native-code/JIT emission, old-generation compaction, concurrent sweep, or changing shapes/codes/realms to nursery allocation without profile evidence.

Child issues cover B1 nursery arena, B2 remaining nursery-aware domains, B3 card-marking barrier, and B4 promotion/tenuring policy.
Minor-GC and nursery metrics are exposed in benchmark reports by the end of the epic.

Relax property inline-cache megamorphic cliff
description: The review identifies a hard polymorphic inline-cache cliff. Current crates/lyng-js/vm/src/vm/feedback.rs sets POLYMORPHIC_PROPERTY_CACHE_LIMIT to 4 and promote_to_megamorphic clears cached entries. This loses useful shape feedback for realistic polymorphic property sites. Raise or redesign the limit and keep enough feedback to fast-path common shapes without compromising invalidation correctness.
acceptance: Create a targeted benchmark or Test262-derived workload with more than four receiver shapes at the same named/keyed property site. Raise the polymorphic capacity or add a compact fallback cache, preserving dependency invalidation and stale-shape rejection. Continue recording diagnostics for monomorphic, polymorphic, and megamorphic states. Add VM feedback tests and verify with cargo test -p lyng-js-vm plus the selected object/class benchmark before and after.

comments.author: codex
comments.text:
Implemented the IC cliff relaxation with TDD coverage. Red evidence before the change: six-shape named and keyed property IC tests both fell to Megamorphic with zero entries, and the feedback snapshot expected Polymorphic but observed Megamorphic.

Changes: raised the polymorphic property cache capacity from 4 to 8, kept promotion to Megamorphic beyond capacity with a 10-shape regression test, and added receiver-shape prefiltering before full cache validation so extra polymorphic entries do not force expensive validation on nonmatching shapes. Matching entries still go through the existing named/keyed cache validation path, preserving stale-shape and invalidation checks. Added a synthetic polymorphic-property-loop benchmark plus synthetic --filter support for compare workloads.

Benchmark evidence: before capacity change, polymorphic-property-loop smoke compare reported lyng-js median 13.167ms / 1.91x quickjs; after the capacity increase plus shape prefilter, it reported 13.261ms / 1.91x quickjs. Boa comparison still fails locally in the existing system-configuration startup path.

Verification: cargo test -p lyng-js-vm six_shape_polymorphic_cache -- --nocapture; cargo test -p lyng-js-vm feedback_vector_snapshot_reports_property_cache_state_without_mutable_entries -- --nocapture; cargo test -p lyng-js-vm named_property_load_ic_promotes_to_megamorphic_beyond_polymorphic_capacity -- --nocapture; cargo test -p lyng-js-vm; cargo test -p lyng-js-bench; cargo clippy -p lyng-js-vm -p lyng-js-bench --all-targets -- -W clippy::pedantic -W clippy::nursery; cargo fmt --all; git diff --check.

Add hot constant and Smi arithmetic bytecode specializations
description: The review finds that tight numeric loops pay for generic LoadSmi and Add/Sub/Mul paths on every iteration. Current crates/lyng-js/bytecode/src/opcode.rs has LoadSmi plus generic arithmetic opcodes and no LoadZero, LoadOne, AddSmi, SubSmi, MulSmi, EqualZero, or LessThanZero forms. Add a limited set of spec-preserving hot opcodes that reduce dispatch and register traffic for common constants and Smi-immediate arithmetic.
acceptance: Add focused opcodes and VM handlers only for measured hot forms. Teach the compiler or a peephole pass to emit them for representative loops without changing observable coercion order. Add bytecode/compiler/VM tests for emitted forms and fallback paths. Verify with cargo test -p lyng-js-compiler and cargo test -p lyng-js-vm, then rerun compare arithmetic-loop and record the delta.

comments.author: 5341456+Feryla@users.noreply.github.com
comments.text: Implemented focused Smi immediate bytecode forms: LoadZero/LoadOne plus AddSmi/SubSmi/MulSmi/DivSmi/ModSmi/BitAndSmi and EqualZero. Compiler emits them only for right-hand i16 numeric literals and === 0, preserving left-to-right evaluation and avoiding loose-equality coercion changes; VM handlers keep Smi/Number fast paths and fall back to normal numeric/add coercions for non-number left values. Added bytecode form/disassembly test, compiler emission test for benchmark-shaped loops, and VM execution/fallback test. Verification: red tests failed on missing opcode variants before implementation; cargo test -p lyng-js-bytecode passed 28 tests plus doc tests; cargo test -p lyng-js-compiler passed 61 tests plus doc tests; cargo test -p lyng-js-vm passed 328 tests plus doc tests; clippy passed for bytecode/compiler/vm with pedantic+nursery; cargo fmt --all and git diff --check passed. Benchmark: prior-change baseline /tmp/lyng-js-4se9-current-array-object.md arithmetic-loop Lyng 7.841ms. Current /tmp/lyng-js-26wf-current-arithmetic-s11-v2.md with --samples 11 --warmup-samples 3 arithmetic-loop Lyng 7.759ms; about 1.05 percent faster. QuickJS/Boa comparison was noisy; local Boa still fails in system-configuration init.

Prototype threaded VM dispatch for interpreter hot path
description: Third-party review /tmp/lyng-js-engine-comparison.md identifies the current giant match in crates/lyng-js/vm/src/vm/dispatch.rs as a dispatch-bound cost. Current tree still fetches Instruction and dispatches through nested matches in Vm::run. The work is to benchmark and prototype a Rust-friendly threaded or function-pointer dispatch path, with a fallback to measured smaller-switch refactors if function-pointer tail calls do not hold up.
acceptance: Establish a release-mode baseline for synthetic compare arithmetic-loop plus one relevant Test262 runtime slice before changing dispatch. Implement an A/B switch or isolated branch for the new dispatch design. Preserve bytecode semantics and VM error behavior. Rerun the same benchmarks and cargo test -p lyng-js-vm, recording deltas and any code-size or profiler tradeoffs in the issue before setting in_review.

comments.author: 5341456+Feryla@users.noreply.github.com
comments.text: Implemented an A/B VM dispatch mode for the interpreter hot path. Vm now exposes VmDispatchMode with the default match loop plus FunctionTable mode, selectable programmatically or with LYNG_JS_VM_DISPATCH=function-table. The function-table path uses a uniform function-pointer handler ABI for hot loop opcodes: loads, env/global slots, arithmetic/comparison ABC value ops, jumps, closure creation, calls, and returns, with fallback to the existing match loop for unsupported opcode families. Added a red-first VM test for selecting FunctionTable mode and executing installed bytecode; the red failure was missing VmDispatchMode plus dispatch_mode/set_dispatch_mode APIs. Verification: cargo test -p lyng-js-vm passed 329 tests plus doc tests; LYNG_JS_VM_DISPATCH=function-table cargo test -p lyng-js-vm passed 329 tests plus doc tests; cargo clippy -p lyng-js-vm --all-targets -- -W clippy::pedantic -W clippy::nursery passed; cargo fmt --all and git diff --check passed. Baseline before dispatch changes: /tmp/lyng-js-2hhp-baseline-arithmetic.md arithmetic-loop Lyng 11.902ms, QuickJS 6.545ms, Boa failed in system-configuration init; Test262 language/statements/for inner-loop baseline /tmp/lyng-js-2hhp-baseline-test262-for.md slowest median 39.340ms, bytecode_execution dominated. Current rebuilt binary: match mode /tmp/lyng-js-2hhp-current-match-arithmetic.md arithmetic-loop Lyng 7.805ms; function-table mode /tmp/lyng-js-2hhp-function-table-arithmetic.md arithmetic-loop Lyng 7.809ms, effectively neutral versus match mode in this run. Function-table Test262 /tmp/lyng-js-2hhp-function-table-test262-for.md slowest median 36.121ms, bytecode_execution dominated. The synthetic compare --filter still emitted all synthetic workloads, so recorded the arithmetic row. Release CLI size was 5,375,536 bytes before rebuild and 5,375,536 bytes after rebuild, plus 0 bytes. No profiler sample was captured; benchmark evidence suggests the function-pointer path is not an arithmetic-loop win on this hardware, so it should stay behind the switch.

Inline small shape transition cache before HashMap fallback
description: The review identifies named-property shape transitions as paying a HashMap lookup on every add-property transition. Current ShapeMetadata in crates/lyng-js/objects/src/object_metadata.rs stores transitions as a HashMap, and ObjectRuntime::transition_shape in crates/lyng-js/objects/src/runtime.rs probes and inserts there. description:

Add background sweep thread infrastructure
description:
Move old-generation sweep work to a background thread after incremental marking has completed its stop-the-world finish. The mutator should resume user code while sweep proceeds, with synchronization around pages/domains whose free lists may be reused.

Scope: add a concurrent_sweep module, spawn one background worker per agent or cluster, make slot-arena free-list interactions thread-safe, and require sweep completion before allocation reuses affected pages.

Out of scope: concurrent marking, old-generation compaction, native-code/JIT emission.

Add Dijkstra barrier for incremental marking
description:
Extend HeapWriter with the incremental-marking barrier needed when the mutator writes a white reference into a black object during marking. Use the Dijkstra model: the white referent is marked gray so the marker cannot miss it.

Why: incremental marking is unsound without a write barrier. Mutator writes can otherwise hide live objects after their owner has already been blackened.

Scope: add barrier state checks to HeapWriter::write_ref/write_value; make the common non-marking and same-generation cases short-circuit cheaply; add stress tests for writes during marking.

Out of scope: SATB barrier model, concurrent marker thread, native-code/JIT emission.

Steady-state runtime benchmark overhead is under 3% on relevant rows when incremental marking is inactive or in common short-circuit paths.

title: Improve V8 v7 RegExp execution throughput
Reduce call-frame hot-path size and register-stack resize churn
description: The review flags VM call-entry overhead from large frame records and register-stack resizing. Current VM code keeps FrameRecord values in the VM frame stack and finish_frame truncates register_stack on return, while call entry grows the same Vec for each activation. For call-heavy workloads, the hot path should push a compact frame header and use a cursor or preallocated register window where that is simpler and measurable.
acceptance: Measure a call-heavy workload before changing frame layout. Identify which FrameRecord fields are needed per dispatch versus only for exceptions, generators, environments, or debugging. Prototype a compact hot frame header or register-stack cursor without weakening rooting, unwinding, for-in/iterator state cleanup, or mapped-arguments finalization. Verify with cargo test -p lyng-js-vm and a call-heavy benchmark, recording memory and runtime deltas.

title: Reduce call-frame hot-path size and register-stack resize churn
Replace builtin dispatch cascades with direct dispatch tables
description: The review identifies builtin dispatch overhead from sequential family checks. Current crates/lyng-js/builtins/src/public/dispatch.rs has a small fast_public_builtin_family shortcut, then walks many dispatch_*_builtin family functions until one handles the BuiltinFunctionId. A direct table or generated family map can reduce overhead for builtin-heavy string, regexp, URI, array, and Temporal paths while keeping builtins organized by domain.
acceptance: Profile a builtin-heavy workload before implementation, such as builtin-string-regexp-loop or a URI/string Test262 slice. Build a table-driven dispatch or family-index mapping for BuiltinFunctionId that avoids the sequential cascade for hot and common builtins. Preserve public/internal builtin separation, realm-aware context behavior, and existing family modules. Add tests for representative builtin IDs across several families and verify with cargo test -p lyng-js-tests plus the selected benchmark before and after.

title: Replace builtin dispatch cascades with direct dispatch tables
Add small-arity call opcodes for common call sites
description: The review identifies call overhead from the generic Call path. Current bytecode exposes Call, CallMethod, TailCall, and Construct, and BytecodeBuilder::emit_call stores argument ranges rather than specialized 0/1/2/3-argument forms. Common JavaScript calls with small arity can avoid range decoding and some call setup if represented by dedicated opcodes or an equivalent compact metadata path.
acceptance: Measure a call-heavy benchmark such as EarleyBoyer or an extracted small-arity call loop before implementation. Add small-arity call forms or a proven equivalent that preserves receiver, spread, Function.prototype.call, bound function, proxy, constructor, and tail-call semantics. Add compiler and VM tests for zero through three arguments plus fallback CallN. Verify with cargo test -p lyng-js-compiler and cargo test -p lyng-js-vm, then rerun the selected call benchmark.

Use hashed storage for WeakSet membership
description: The review points out that WeakSet membership is linear. acceptance: Replace or augment WeakSetState storage with a hash-based representation that preserves weak liveness filtering, deterministic behavior expected by tests, and delete semantics. Add tests for insert, duplicate insert, contains, delete, and retain_live_values. Verify with cargo test -p lyng-js-vm or the owning GC/builtin tests, plus a small WeakSet microbenchmark if available.

Audit allocation and reference-write sites
description:
Audit every Lyng JS heap allocation entry point and every write of a heap reference into a heap-resident record before adding nursery or write-barrier behavior. Produce docs/lyng-js/gc-write-sites.md grouped by record family and crate/module, with each site tagged for whether it will need a future barrier.

Why: generational GC correctness depends on a complete list of old-to-young reference writes. A missed heap-reference write can make a future card-marking barrier unsound.

Relevant areas: crates/lyng-js/gc/, crates/lyng-js/objects/, crates/lyng-js/env/, crates/lyng-js/vm/, feedback entries, object slots, environment slots, and records containing Value/ObjectRef/StringRef/SymbolRef/BigIntRef/EnvironmentRef/CodeRef/ShapeId.

Out of scope: adding the barrier or refactoring call sites.
acceptance:
docs/lyng-js/gc-write-sites.md exists and lists every allocation/write site grouped by record family and crate/module.
Each documented site states whether a future write barrier is expected.
A small Clippy lint or grep script under tools/ fails CI when a new direct Value/Ref write to a heap field appears outside the documented set.
No engine behavior changes are made.

title: Audit allocation and reference-write sites
Introduce HeapWriter mutator chokepoint
description:
Add a single API for writing heap references into heap-resident locations and route the A1 audited sites through it. The initial implementation is a pass-through so this issue is a mechanical refactor, not a collector semantic change.

Why: future card-marking and incremental-marking barriers need one airtight mutator chokepoint. Deferring barrier behavior until the call-site shape is stable lowers risk.

Scope: define write_ref<T: HeapRef>(slot: &mut T, value: T) and matching write_value on the existing PrimitiveMutator/HeapWriter path; replace direct writes identified by A1 across gc, objects, env, and vm.

Out of scope: nursery allocation, promotion, card marking, incremental marker barriers, or changing observable JavaScript behavior.
acceptance:
cargo test -p lyng-js-tests passes or any pre-existing failures are documented with baseline evidence.
cargo test -p lyng-js-vm passes.
lyng-js-bench runtime shows no regression on dense-indexed and class-heavy rows outside sample noise.
The A1 direct-write lint reports zero undocumented direct-write sites remaining.

title: Migrate remaining domains to nursery-aware allocation
Add card-marking write barrier
description:
Replace the pass-through HeapWriter with a real card-marking barrier for old-generation writes that store young-generation references. Minor GC should scan dirty cards plus roots instead of scanning the whole old generation.

Why: without remembered sets, every minor GC must search all old-generation records for old-to-young pointers, erasing the nursery benefit and risking missed references if the scan is incomplete.

Scope: add a CardTable keyed by old-generation page/card index, update HeapWriter::write_ref/write_value to mark cards for old-to-young writes, and update minor-GC root scanning to consume dirty cards.

Out of scope: Dijkstra/SATB incremental-marking barrier behavior, concurrent marking, and native-code/JIT emission.
acceptance:
Minor-GC scan time scales with dirty-card count rather than total old-generation size.
Benchmark output reports cards dirtied per minor GC.
Tests cover old-to-young reference preservation through object slots, environment slots, and feedback/side-table paths.
Test262 pass rate is unchanged, or unrelated baseline failures are documented.

title: Slice major-GC mark phase
Add Dijkstra barrier for incremental marking
description:
Extend HeapWriter with the incremental-marking barrier needed when the mutator writes a white reference into a black object during marking. Use the Dijkstra model: the white referent is marked gray so the marker cannot miss it.

Why: incremental marking is unsound without a write barrier. Mutator writes can otherwise hide live objects after their owner has already been blackened.

Scope: add barrier state checks to HeapWriter::write_ref/write_value; make the common non-marking and same-generation cases short-circuit cheaply; add stress tests for writes during marking.

Out of scope: SATB barrier model, concurrent marker thread, native-code/JIT emission.
acceptance:
Steady-state runtime benchmark overhead is under 3% on relevant rows when incremental marking is inactive or in common short-circuit paths.
Differential testing against pre-C2 behavior shows identical JavaScript results.
Tests demonstrate that writes into black objects preserve newly-referenced white objects.
Test262 pass rate is unchanged, or unrelated baseline failures are documented.

title: JIT-ready incremental marking
Add background sweep thread infrastructure
description:
Move old-generation sweep work to a background thread after incremental marking has completed its stop-the-world finish. The mutator should resume user code while sweep proceeds, with synchronization around pages/domains whose free lists may be reused.

Why: sweep is a significant component of pause time. Once C3 has produced a completed mark set, sweep can run off the mutator thread if free-list reuse is synchronized precisely.

Scope: add a concurrent_sweep module, spawn one background worker per agent or cluster, make slot-arena free-list interactions thread-safe, and require sweep completion before allocation reuses affected pages.

Out of scope: concurrent marking, old-generation compaction, native-code/JIT emission.
acceptance:
Benchmark/report output shows sweep running on the background thread and main-thread pause limited to the mark finish step.
Test262 pass rate is unchanged, or unrelated baseline failures are documented.
High-allocation stress/fuzz testing is stable for at least one hour.
Synchronization rules are documented near the sweep implementation.

title: Add background sweep thread infrastructure
Define concurrent sweep weak-ref correctness
description:
Audit and document how concurrent sweep interacts with WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry lifecycle handling. Define when weak refs are cleared, when finalization callbacks are enqueued, and which host-visible ordering is guaranteed.

Why: concurrent sweep changes timing around object death. Weak references and finalizers are guest-observable, so the collector ordering must be precise before sweep runs off-thread.

Scope: review crates/lyng-js/gc/src/collection.rs weak-ref and FinalizationRegistry paths, update or create docs/lyng-js/gc.md with lifecycle rules, and add focused coverage for the new ordering.

Out of scope: changing JavaScript WeakRef semantics beyond what concurrent sweep requires, native-code/JIT emission.
acceptance:
Test262 WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry coverage passes, or unrelated baseline failures are documented.
docs/lyng-js/gc.md describes weak-reference clearing and finalizer enqueue ordering under concurrent sweep.
Tests cover weak refs/finalizers across mark finish and background sweep boundaries.

title: Slice major-GC mark phase
Add background sweep thread infrastructure
description:
Move old-generation sweep work to a background thread after incremental marking has completed its stop-the-world finish. The mutator should resume user code while sweep proceeds, with synchronization around pages/domains whose free lists may be reused.

Why: sweep is a significant component of pause time. Once C3 has produced a completed mark set, sweep can run off the mutator thread if free-list reuse is synchronized precisely.

Scope: add a concurrent_sweep module, spawn one background worker per agent or cluster, make slot-arena free-list interactions thread-safe, and require sweep completion before allocation reuses affected pages.

Out of scope: concurrent marking, old-generation compaction, native-code/JIT emission.

Add inspector frame-inspection skeleton
description:
Add a minimal debugger/inspector surface for pause, resume, stepping, frame enumeration, register reads, and environment-slot reads. Implement it as a host/debug trait with near-zero overhead when no debugger is attached.

Why: debugger hooks should exist before JIT tiers complicate execution. A stable interpreter-level inspection contract makes future tier integration easier and testable.

Scope: add a debug crate/module or host-owned trait; poll a debug-pause flag at function-entry and LoopHeader safepoints; expose pause, resume, step_in, step_out, step_over, enumerate_frames, read_register, and read_env_slot; define step-over/out in terms of frame count.

Out of scope: full Chrome DevTools Protocol, source-level breakpoints, source maps, watch expressions, evaluate-in-frame, or JIT code generation.
acceptance:
A test embedder can pause at a specified bytecode offset, enumerate frames, read register values, and resume.
Step over/out/in behavior is defined and covered at bytecode/frame level.
With debugger disabled, per-opcode dispatch overhead is at most 1% versus baseline.
The API preserves crate boundaries between host/debugger and VM internals.

title: JIT-ready observability and tooling
JIT-ready deopt invariant enforcement
description:
Make existing DeoptSnapshot, SafepointDescriptor, and RuntimeStateCapture metadata load-bearing through debug-build round-trip assertions.

Why: the metadata exists today but is not exercised. If opcode additions and abstract operations let the frame-state contract drift, a later JIT will inherit stale deoptimization metadata that is too broken to trust.

Out of scope: actually bailing out from native code, machine-code generation, or optimizer IR.
acceptance:
Child issue F1 verifies interpreter frame state at safepoints in debug builds.
Diagnostics precisely identify snapshot/frame mismatches.
Debug and release verification remain green for the affected test suites.

title: JIT-ready deopt invariant enforcement
Add debug-build deopt round-trip assertions
description:
At every interpreter SafepointDescriptor position, debug builds should materialize the declared RuntimeStateCapture and DeoptSnapshot, compare it to the current interpreter frame state, and panic with a precise diagnostic on mismatch.

Why: safepoint/deopt metadata exists today but is not exercised. Debug assertions make the frame-state contract load-bearing before any future JIT depends on it.

Scope: implement a materialize-snapshot helper in crates/lyng-js/vm/src/vm/state.rs or equivalent; insert assertions at allocation, loop-backedge, and exception-edge safepoint poll sites; add fixtures that exercise opcodes with debug assertions enabled.

Out of scope: native-code bailout, optimized-frame reconstruction, optimizer IR, or JIT code generation.
acceptance:
cargo test -p lyng-js-vm passes in debug profile.
cargo test -p lyng-js-tests passes in debug profile, or unrelated baseline failures are documented.
A deliberately-broken local test demonstrates that mismatched live frame state fails with a clear diagnostic.
Release builds do not pay runtime overhead for the assertion path.

description:
Second-phase performance epic on top of lyng-4dwr.

Third-party engine comparison (lyng-js vs QuickJS, V8 jitless, JSC LLInt) finds that lyng-js sits ~1.94x-2.38x slower than QuickJS across the synthetic compare corpus and consistently across V8 v7 Octane-style workloads (Richards 4.90x, DeltaBlue 4.23x, RayTrace 2.96x, Splay 2.04x, NavierStokes 5.03x, Crypto 6.72x, RegExp 3.06x, EarleyBoyer 5.15x — from the lyng-4dwr-c2 comment). The previous performance round (Phase 1) closed major obvious items: threaded dispatch prototype (lyng-2hhp, neutral result), Smi/constant specializations (lyng-26wf, +1%), poly IC limit relaxation (lyng-1xig, neutral), call-frame hot-path size reduction (lyng-3wvk), shape-transition cache (lyng-4se9), register access bounds elimination (lyng-5zky), peephole pass (lyng-458m), small-arity call opcodes (lyng-4zvc), builtin dispatch tables (lyng-473x), megamorphic relaxation (lyng-46rj), dense-index feedback (lyng-60hn), cons strings (lyng-5j2i), and others.

The gap that remains is structural — dispatch + decode overhead distributed across the hot path. The two structural costs are:

1. Bytecode storage is `Vec<Instruction>` where `Instruction` is a Rust enum with discriminant + Ax-form padding. Confirmed by mock compile: `size_of::<Instruction>() == 8` bytes on aarch64-darwin. The on-wire encoding is 4 bytes; the in-memory layout is 8. Every dispatch does `instructions.get(idx).copied()` reading 8 bytes from an arbitrary heap location, then matches on the enum discriminant, then matches on the inner opcode. QuickJS averages 1.5-2 bytes/op via variable-width byte streams; V8 averages similar via accumulator-based ISA with operand-scale prefixes. lyng-js pushes 3-5x more bytes through the I-cache for typical inner loops.

2. Feedback-bearing opcodes look up their IC slot via `(CodeRef, instruction_offset) -> slot` map at every execution (record_feedback_site). V8 encodes the slot index directly in the bytecode operand of the IC-bearing opcode so `feedback_vector[slot_id]` is a single indexed load. JSC's LLInt uses per-bytecode metadata indexed by bytecode offset, achieving the same result.

This epic addresses both of those, plus three smaller items in the same hot loop:

- Add more short-form opcodes (8-bit jump deltas, register-implicit LocalN access) building on lyng-26wf
- Improve polymorphic IC lookup data structure (keep the 8-entry limit set in lyng-1xig but replace the linear scan with a hashed/branched lookup)
- Hoist hot frame state into the dispatch loop's locals, building on lyng-3wvk

Expected combined impact: close roughly half of the QuickJS gap (target arithmetic-loop median below 4.0ms vs current 5.66ms; QuickJS at 2.91ms).

Sources:
- Third-party engine analysis: /tmp/lyng-js-engine-analysis.md (in-session)
- Existing perf epic: lyng-4dwr
- Pending bytecode density evaluation: lyng-5u2z (this epic supersedes that)
acceptance: All five sub-issues land with measured before/after evidence in their dcat handoffs. The combined compare-corpus medians on arithmetic-loop, array-object-loop, and builtin-string-regexp-loop show a measurable improvement vs. the 2026-05-12 baseline of 5.66ms / 8.29ms / 18.46ms. Test262 pass count remains unchanged from the current whole-suite baseline. The bytecode-density report shows reduced encoded-byte totals consistent with the encoding change in 1.1 and short-form additions in 1.2. V8 v7 Richards / DeltaBlue / NavierStokes ratios drop from the May 2026 baselines recorded in lyng-4dwr-c2.
