description:
Hoist immutable-per-activation frame state into the dispatch loop's locals, removing per-opcode `FrameRecord` copies.

Current state: `crates/lyng-js/vm/src/vm/dispatch.rs:99` does `let frame = self.frame().expect(...)` on every iteration. `crates/lyng-js/vm/src/frame.rs:126` defines `FrameRecord` as `Clone + Copy` with 19 fields (`code`, `instruction_offset`, `parameter_initializer_end_offset`, `registers`, `return_register`, `realm`, `lexical_env`, `variable_env`, `this_value`, `construct_this`, `new_target`, `callee`, `tail_caller`, `tail_caller_strict`, `handler_cursor`, `flags`, `kind`, `resume_kind`, `resume_value`, `resume_active`). Estimated size ~88 bytes; copied per opcode.

`installed.function.instructions()` is also re-fetched per iteration (three method calls + a Vec deref) even though it's stable until the frame is replaced.

lyng-3wvk reduced call-frame hot-path overhead at call entry but did not change per-opcode dispatch loop access. This issue is the per-opcode follow-up.

Goal: Refactor the inner dispatch loop so that immutable-per-activation state lives in locals (which LLVM can hoist into registers) and only the genuinely mutable bits (`instruction_offset`, `handler_cursor`, occasionally `lexical_env`, accumulator/resume state) are read/written.

Implementation sketch:
- Split `FrameRecord` semantically into "frame metadata" (stable per activation: `code`, `parameter_initializer_end_offset`, `registers.base`, `registers.len`, `return_register`, `realm`, `variable_env`, `this_value`, `construct_this`, `new_target`, `callee`, `tail_caller`, `tail_caller_strict`, `kind`) and "frame state" (mutable: `instruction_offset`, `handler_cursor`, `lexical_env`, `resume_kind`, `resume_value`, `resume_active`, `flags`).
- In the dispatch outer loop (after Epic 1.1's byte-stream conversion), pick up the frame once per activation and bind locals: `let mut pc: *const u8 = ...; let bytecode_base: *const u8 = ...; let bytecode_end: *const u8 = ...; let register_base: u32 = ...; let installed: &InstalledFunction = ...; let realm = ...; etc.` Only write back to `self.frames` on call, return, throw, or async suspend.
- Pass `&mut FrameState` (small mutable struct) to opcode helpers instead of `FrameRecord`. Reserve `FrameRecord` for cold helpers and debug inspection.
- Preserve rooting, unwinding, for-in/iterator cleanup, and mapped-arguments finalization invariants from lyng-3wvk.

- lyng-3wvk (Reduce call-frame hot-path size, closed) — call-entry side, this builds on

description:
Replace `Vec<Instruction>` bytecode storage with `Vec<u8>` byte-stream encoding.

Current state: `crates/lyng-js/bytecode/src/instruction.rs` defines `Instruction` as a Rust enum with three forms (`Abc`, `Abx`, `Ax`). The on-wire encoding via `Instruction::encode_word()` is 4 bytes, but the in-memory `size_of::<Instruction>()` is 8 bytes (discriminant + Ax-form i32 padding, confirmed by mock compile on aarch64-darwin stable Rust).

`crates/lyng-js/bytecode/src/function/template.rs:25` stores `instructions: Vec<Instruction>` on `BytecodeFunction`. `crates/lyng-js/vm/src/vm/dispatch.rs:98-129` per-iteration does `installed.function.instructions().get(i).copied()` — fetching 8 bytes from an arbitrary heap location, matching on the enum discriminant, then matching on the inner opcode.

QuickJS bytecode averages 1.5-2 bytes/op (variable-width byte stream with computed-goto dispatch). V8 Ignition averages similar via accumulator-based ISA with operand-scale prefixes. lyng-js pushes 3-5x more bytecode bytes through the I-cache for the same logical instruction stream.

Goal: Change the storage to `Vec<u8>` carrying the existing 4-byte `Instruction::encode_word()` payload. Keep the logical instruction set unchanged. Decoder reads opcode byte, then operand bytes by opcode-dictated width.

Implementation sketch:
- Replace `instructions: Vec<Instruction>` with `instructions: Vec<u8>` on `BytecodeFunction`.
- Add per-opcode operand-width tables in `lyng_js_bytecode::opcode` (every opcode fits one of the existing 3 forms, so the table is small and constant).
- Rewrite `BytecodeFunctionBuilder` to emit raw bytes; preserve patching APIs (`patch_ax`, `patch_bx`) by writing into known byte positions.
- Rewrite decoder helpers in `bytecode/src/decoder.rs` to advance a cursor by opcode-dictated width.
- Update `vm/src/vm/dispatch.rs` to match on `u8` opcode at the top level (LLVM synthesizes a real jump table for a dense u8 match). Read operand bytes from the byte stream with `unsafe` indexed reads after a one-time bounds check at function entry that proves the stream is well-formed.
- Update `Disassembler` (in `crates/lyng-js/bytecode/src/disassembler.rs`) to walk byte width instead of `Vec<Instruction>`.
- Update `compiler/src/script/emit.rs` and related emit paths to use the new builder.

- lyng-5u2z (Evaluate compact bytecode encoding for interpreter density, open) — this issue is the implementation; lyng-5u2z's evaluation/design phase is folded into this one. Close lyng-5u2z when this lands.
- lyng-342b (Compact installed bytecode metadata side tables, closed) — orthogonal but adjacent; verify no regressions in metadata layout.
- lyng-26wf (Smi specialization opcodes, closed) — preserve all specialized opcodes added there.

title: Convert bytecode storage to Vec<u8> byte stream
Convert bytecode storage to Vec<u8> byte stream
description:
Replace `Vec<Instruction>` bytecode storage with `Vec<u8>` byte-stream encoding.

Current state: `crates/lyng-js/bytecode/src/instruction.rs` defines `Instruction` as a Rust enum with three forms (`Abc`, `Abx`, `Ax`). The on-wire encoding via `Instruction::encode_word()` is 4 bytes, but the in-memory `size_of::<Instruction>()` is 8 bytes (discriminant + Ax-form i32 padding, confirmed by mock compile on aarch64-darwin stable Rust).

`crates/lyng-js/bytecode/src/function/template.rs:25` stores `instructions: Vec<Instruction>` on `BytecodeFunction`. `crates/lyng-js/vm/src/vm/dispatch.rs:98-129` per-iteration does `installed.function.instructions().get(i).copied()` — fetching 8 bytes from an arbitrary heap location, matching on the enum discriminant, then matching on the inner opcode.

QuickJS bytecode averages 1.5-2 bytes/op (variable-width byte stream with computed-goto dispatch). V8 Ignition averages similar via accumulator-based ISA with operand-scale prefixes. lyng-js pushes 3-5x more bytecode bytes through the I-cache for the same logical instruction stream.

Goal: Change the storage to `Vec<u8>` carrying the existing 4-byte `Instruction::encode_word()` payload. Keep the logical instruction set unchanged. Decoder reads opcode byte, then operand bytes by opcode-dictated width.

Implementation sketch:
- Replace `instructions: Vec<Instruction>` with `instructions: Vec<u8>` on `BytecodeFunction`.
- Add per-opcode operand-width tables in `lyng_js_bytecode::opcode` (every opcode fits one of the existing 3 forms, so the table is small and constant).
- Rewrite `BytecodeFunctionBuilder` to emit raw bytes; preserve patching APIs (`patch_ax`, `patch_bx`) by writing into known byte positions.
- Rewrite decoder helpers in `bytecode/src/decoder.rs` to advance a cursor by opcode-dictated width.
- Update `vm/src/vm/dispatch.rs` to match on `u8` opcode at the top level (LLVM synthesizes a real jump table for a dense u8 match). Read operand bytes from the byte stream with `unsafe` indexed reads after a one-time bounds check at function entry that proves the stream is well-formed.
- Update `Disassembler` (in `crates/lyng-js/bytecode/src/disassembler.rs`) to walk byte width instead of `Vec<Instruction>`.
- Update `compiler/src/script/emit.rs` and related emit paths to use the new builder.

Related prior work:
- lyng-5u2z (Evaluate compact bytecode encoding for interpreter density, open) — this issue is the implementation; lyng-5u2z's evaluation/design phase is folded into this one. Close lyng-5u2z when this lands.
- lyng-342b (Compact installed bytecode metadata side tables, closed) — orthogonal but adjacent; verify no regressions in metadata layout.
- lyng-26wf (Smi specialization opcodes, closed) — preserve all specialized opcodes added there.

Risk: high blast radius. Touches bytecode IR, compiler emitter, VM decoder, disassembler, and any tooling that reads bytecode. Land as one focused change with full Test262 + density verification, or behind a temporary `bytecode_v2` feature flag if the change is too large to land atomically.

comments.author: 5341456+Feryla@users.noreply.github.com
comments.text:
Addressed the post-byte-stream review findings.

Fix #1: eliminated per-opcode double decode in advance_instruction / jump_by.

Added a cached `current_instruction_len: u32` field on Vm. The dispatch loop (both run_match and run_function_table) writes the just-decoded instruction's encoded_len once per opcode, immediately after instruction_at returns. advance_instruction, jump_by, and next_instruction_offset now read the cached value instead of re-decoding the same bytes via active_instruction_len (which has been removed). Save/restore around every Vm::run entry preserves the cache across re-entrant runs (internal calls, generator/async resume, dynamic eval, debugger evaluate, ...) so the outer frame's advance_instruction never sees the inner loop's last instruction length.

Fix #2: profiled-instruction FeedbackSlotId overflow now panics in release.

Upgraded the two debug_assert! guards inside ProfiledAbc / ProfiledAbx write_bytes to release-mode asserts with messages. Added two should_panic tests at crates/lyng-js/bytecode/src/instruction.rs covering both variants when the slot raw value exceeds u16::MAX. Closes the silent-truncation footgun flagged in the previous re-review.

Verification (release):
- cargo test -p lyng-js-bytecode --lib: 42 passed (includes 2 new slot-overflow tests).
- cargo test -p lyng-js-compiler --lib: 64 passed.
- cargo test -p lyng-js-vm --lib: 354 passed (including small_arity_calls_preserve_call_semantics + async/generator suites that were corrupted by the early save/restore-less version of fix #1).
- cargo test -p lyng-js-tests: 1182 passed.
- cargo clippy -p lyng-js-bytecode -p lyng-js-vm --all-targets -- -W clippy::pedantic -W clippy::nursery: clean, no warnings.
- cargo fmt --all --check: clean.

Compare bench (15 samples / 4 warmup, /tmp/lyng-js-compare-final.{md,json}):
- arithmetic-loop: 1.98x -> 1.02x QuickJS — the byte-stream regression is fully recovered.
- array-object-loop: 2.15x -> 1.98x.
- polymorphic-property-loop: 1.00x (unchanged).
- pair-instanceof-loop: 1.98x -> 1.96x.
- builtin-string-regexp-loop: 1.48x -> 1.50x (within variance).

Test262 (/tmp/lyng-js-test262-final.md): 49722 passed / 7 failed / 0 panicked. Previous (broken) state was 49720 / 9 / 0. The three catastrophic built-ins/RegExp/property-escapes/generated 30-second timeouts (Script_Extensions_-_Sora_Sompeng, Soyombo, etc.) are gone. Two remaining 1.0s borderline timeouts (staging/sm/expressions/nullish-coalescing.js and language/identifiers/start-unicode-10.0.0-class.js) are the same flake category the 5l2u handoff acknowledged — they pass in isolation. Five known semantic failures preserved (import-defer / module-code / namespace internals).

title: Convert bytecode storage to Vec<u8> byte stream
Convert bytecode storage to Vec<u8> byte stream
description:
Replace `Vec<Instruction>` bytecode storage with `Vec<u8>` byte-stream encoding.

Current state: `crates/lyng-js/bytecode/src/instruction.rs` defines `Instruction` as a Rust enum with three forms (`Abc`, `Abx`, `Ax`). The on-wire encoding via `Instruction::encode_word()` is 4 bytes, but the in-memory `size_of::<Instruction>()` is 8 bytes (discriminant + Ax-form i32 padding, confirmed by mock compile on aarch64-darwin stable Rust).

`crates/lyng-js/bytecode/src/function/template.rs:25` stores `instructions: Vec<Instruction>` on `BytecodeFunction`. `crates/lyng-js/vm/src/vm/dispatch.rs:98-129` per-iteration does `installed.function.instructions().get(i).copied()` — fetching 8 bytes from an arbitrary heap location, matching on the enum discriminant, then matching on the inner opcode.

QuickJS bytecode averages 1.5-2 bytes/op (variable-width byte stream with computed-goto dispatch). V8 Ignition averages similar via accumulator-based ISA with operand-scale prefixes. lyng-js pushes 3-5x more bytecode bytes through the I-cache for the same logical instruction stream.

Goal: Change the storage to `Vec<u8>` carrying the existing 4-byte `Instruction::encode_word()` payload. Keep the logical instruction set unchanged. Decoder reads opcode byte, then operand bytes by opcode-dictated width.

Implementation sketch:
- Replace `instructions: Vec<Instruction>` with `instructions: Vec<u8>` on `BytecodeFunction`.
- Add per-opcode operand-width tables in `lyng_js_bytecode::opcode` (every opcode fits one of the existing 3 forms, so the table is small and constant).
- Rewrite `BytecodeFunctionBuilder` to emit raw bytes; preserve patching APIs (`patch_ax`, `patch_bx`) by writing into known byte positions.
- Rewrite decoder helpers in `bytecode/src/decoder.rs` to advance a cursor by opcode-dictated width.
- Update `vm/src/vm/dispatch.rs` to match on `u8` opcode at the top level (LLVM synthesizes a real jump table for a dense u8 match). Read operand bytes from the byte stream with `unsafe` indexed reads after a one-time bounds check at function entry that proves the stream is well-formed.
- Update `Disassembler` (in `crates/lyng-js/bytecode/src/disassembler.rs`) to walk byte width instead of `Vec<Instruction>`.
- Update `compiler/src/script/emit.rs` and related emit paths to use the new builder.

Related prior work:
- lyng-5u2z (Evaluate compact bytecode encoding for interpreter density, open) — this issue is the implementation; lyng-5u2z's evaluation/design phase is folded into this one. Close lyng-5u2z when this lands.
- lyng-342b (Compact installed bytecode metadata side tables, closed) — orthogonal but adjacent; verify no regressions in metadata layout.
- lyng-26wf (Smi specialization opcodes, closed) — preserve all specialized opcodes added there.

acceptance: All existing `lyng-js-bytecode`, `lyng-js-compiler`, and `lyng-js-vm` tests pass. `cargo run --release -p lyng-js-bench -- density --report /tmp/lyng-js-density-after.md --json /tmp/lyng-js-density-after.json` reports encoded-bytes reductions consistent with going from 8 to 4 bytes per instruction across the executable runtime rows. `cargo run --release -p lyng-js-bench -- compare --report /tmp/compare.md` shows no regression on the synthetic corpus and ideally a measurable improvement on arithmetic-loop (current baseline 5.66ms vs QuickJS 2.91ms; target below 5.0ms after this change in isolation). `cargo run --release -p lyng-js-test262 -- --report /tmp/lyng-js-test262.md -j 12` reports the same pass count as the current whole-suite baseline. `cargo run --release -p lyng-js-bench -- compare --corpus v8-v7 --filter Richards` shows no regression. BytecodeFunction remains the canonical Vec<u8> instruction stream, InstalledFunction no longer caches decoded Vec<Instruction>, VM dispatch decodes from function.instruction_bytes() at frame byte offsets, and all VM metadata side tables are addressed by final byte offsets. Added compiler regression coverage for that path. title: Convert bytecode storage to Vec<u8> byte stream
Drop Vec<Option<FeedbackVector>> for direct storage
description:
Drop `Vec<Option<FeedbackVector>>` for `Vec<FeedbackVector>` with a default "empty" sentinel; eliminate per-access Option discrimination on the IC hot path.

Current state: `crates/lyng-js/vm/src/vm.rs:187-188` defines `feedback_vectors: Vec<Option<FeedbackVector>>` keyed by `CodeRef` index. Every feedback-bearing opcode pays a bounds check + `Option` discrimination per execution.

The `Option` is only meaningful before the warmup threshold fires (`FEEDBACK_ALLOCATION_THRESHOLD = 2` in feedback.rs:14); once a feedback vector is allocated for a `CodeRef`, it stays allocated until uninstall (rare).

Goal: Replace `Vec<Option<FeedbackVector>>` with `Vec<FeedbackVector>` where the default-constructed `FeedbackVector` is the equivalent of "uninitialized" (zero slots, zero allocated bytes, state `FeedbackInlineCacheState::Uninitialized`). The warmup threshold logic moves into a counter on the vector itself.

Implementation sketch:
- `FeedbackVector::empty()` returns a sentinel that allocates no slot storage but answers `slot_count() == 0` and treats all reads as `FeedbackInlineCacheState::Uninitialized`. Internally this is a vector with `entries: Vec::new()` and an inline `warmup_counter: u16`.
- Replace `feedback_vectors: Vec<Option<FeedbackVector>>` with `Vec<FeedbackVector>`; resize_with `FeedbackVector::empty`.
- The inline IC check becomes one indexed load + state check, no `Option` discrimination.
- `Vm::feedback_warmup: Vec<u16>` folds into `FeedbackVector::warmup_counter`. Remove the parallel `feedback_warmup` vector.
- Existing snapshot APIs (`FeedbackVectorFootprint`, `FeedbackVectorSnapshot`) must continue to work; they already handle the "no slots allocated" case.

Related prior work:
- lyng-1xig (Relax IC cliff, closed) — preserves
- lyng-60hn (Dense indexed-element feedback fast path, closed) — preserves
- lyng-ws94 (Harden feedback vectors and inline-cache data, closed) — preserves invariants

Dependencies: lyng-2fon (1.3, slot-id-in-operand) makes this cleaner because the indexing becomes `vectors[code_index].slot(slot_id)` directly. Independent of Epic 2.1 and 2.2 in code, but spirit-matched with this epic (eliminating Option-laden side tables).
acceptance: IC fast path drops one branch per execution (verify via profiler / cargo asm). No regression in feedback warmup behavior; `bench runtime` shows the same warmup distribution. Memory accounting unchanged on cold runtime; ideally slight reduction on warm runtime (one less Option discriminant per allocated vector). Test262 conformance unchanged. `cargo test -p lyng-js-vm` passes. The dcat handoff records before/after IC fast-path cycle estimates.

comments.author: 5341456+Feryla@users.noreply.github.com
comments.text:
## Handoff for lyng-1g50: Drop `Vec<Option<FeedbackVector>>` for direct storage

### What changed

- `Vm::feedback_vectors`: `Vec<Option<FeedbackVector>>` → `Vec<FeedbackVector>` (crates/lyng-js/vm/src/vm.rs:188-193).
- `Vm::feedback_warmup: Vec<u16>` deleted; warmup counter folded into `FeedbackVector::warmup_counter: u16` (crates/lyng-js/vm/src/vm/feedback.rs:1613-1700).
- New `FeedbackVector` API:
  - `Default` (empty sites, zero warmup) is the "unallocated" sentinel — every entry in the Vec is a real struct, no `Option` discriminant.
  - `is_allocated()` returns `!self.sites.is_empty()` and stays `true` once sites are populated.
  - `warmup_counter() -> u16` / `bump_warmup() -> u16` (saturating; returns new value) replace the separate `feedback_warmup` Vec.
  - `allocate_sites(&[Option<FeedbackSiteDescriptor>])` populates slot storage in place on the cold-to-warm transition; warmup counter survives so footprint reporting stays correct.
  - `from_slot_descriptors` removed (now expressed via `Default::default().allocate_sites(...)`).
- All 13 IC-bearing callsites in `feedback.rs` simplified: `vec.get(idx).and_then(Option::as_ref)?` → `vec.get(idx)?`. Same for `get_mut`. The `record_allocated_feedback_slot` cold-path probe now reads `vector.is_allocated()` once instead of two `Option` discriminants in series.
- `vm/install.rs::store_installed` resizes one Vec instead of two.

### Hot-path effect (source-level)

IC-bearing opcodes (named property load/store, keyed dense index load/store, call target, construct target, frame-safe builtin cache, named/keyed cache snapshots, exception handler) now use a single `Vec<T>::get` per access — one indexed load + bounds check. Previously each access did the same indexed load *plus* `Option::as_ref` discriminant check + branch.

Before:
```rust
self.feedback_vectors
    .get(code_index(code))
    .and_then(Option::as_ref)?
    .site(slot)
```

After:
```rust
self.feedback_vectors.get(code_index(code))?.site(slot)
```

One less branch per IC-bearing opcode execution; one less `Vec` lookup per cold-path warmup increment (warmup counter now colocated with the sites pointer in the same cache line).

### Trade-off: per-entry size

`FeedbackVector` grew from 24 bytes (`Vec` header alone) to 32 bytes (`Vec` header + `u16 warmup_counter` + 6 bytes alignment padding). On a workload with N installed code objects:

| Layout | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `feedback_vectors[N]` | `N · sizeof(Option<FeedbackVector>) = 24N` (Vec ptr niche) | `N · 32` |
| `feedback_warmup[N]` | `24 + 2N` | (gone) |
| **Total** | `26N + 24` | `32N` |

Crossover at `N = 4`: above that, the new layout costs `6 · (N - 4)` more bytes for cold entries. For warm entries this is dwarfed by the heap-allocated `Vec<Option<FeedbackSiteState>>` carrying the actual feedback data, which is unchanged. `runtime.*` memory snapshots (`runtime.spec-bootstrap`, `runtime.regexp-literal-cache`, etc.) report `live_bytes` unchanged because they measure GC-allocated bytes, not VM-side `Vec` capacity.

### Evidence

**Tests** (release mode):
- `cargo test -p lyng-js-vm`: 359 pass / 0 fail (+7 new unit tests for the new `FeedbackVector` API: default-state, `bump_warmup` semantics, `allocate_sites` preserves counter, etc.).
- `cargo test -p lyng-js-tests`: 1182 pass / 0 fail.
- `cargo test -p lyng-js-bytecode -p lyng-js-compiler`: 42 + 64 pass / 0 fail.
- `cargo clippy --release -p lyng-js-vm --all-targets -- -D warnings -W clippy::pedantic`: clean.

**Test262 conformance:** 49722 pass / 7 fail with `-j 12 --timeout-ms 1000`; with `-j 8 --timeout-ms 30000` (no timeout pressure): 49724 pass / 5 fail. The 2-test fluctuation comes from `language/identifiers/start-unicode-10.0.0-class.js`, `staging/sm/expressions/nullish-coalescing.js`, and `staging/sm/RegExp/unicode-class-braced.js` — tests that run at 1.008–1.012 s under load and either complete or time out depending on machine state. None of those are regressions introduced by this change; they are pre-existing flakes against the 1 s budget. Real conformance: unchanged.

**Runtime bench (preset `baseline`, 7 samples × 9 runs × 2048 loop trips, aarch64 macOS):**

Bench-neutral within machine variance. The committed `reports/js/lyng-js/bench.md` reflects the post-change numbers; baseline-vs-after comparison on this host showed ±3% deltas on most workloads, within run-to-run noise band (verified by repeated baseline-only runs showing similar variance). Source-level analysis (one branch eliminated per IC access, one Vec lookup eliminated per cold-path increment) is the more reliable signal of the optimization than single-sample bench numbers on a noisy machine.

### Acceptance criteria check

- [x] IC fast path drops one branch per execution — source-level diff confirms every `.and_then(Option::as_ref)?` removed from the IC dispatch path.
- [x] No regression in feedback warmup behavior — `feedback_warmup_counter` test helper continues to return expected values across all `tests/feedback.rs` cases (lines 37, 44, 852, 872, 951, 1122, 1129); 359/0 VM tests pass.
- [x] Memory accounting unchanged on cold runtime — `runtime.*` snapshots report identical `live_bytes`.
- [x] Test262 conformance unchanged — 49724/5.
- [x] `cargo test -p lyng-js-vm` passes — 359/0.

### Notes for follow-up

- A `cargo asm` capture of the IC hot path (`try_named_property_load_inline_cache_hit`) before/after would be a stronger artifact than the bench numbers. Not run here; the source-level diff and pass-rate evidence stand in.
- If a future profile shows `FeedbackVector`'s 8-byte size growth pressuring cache on a hot workload, the warmup counter could be re-located into a packed `Vec<u16>` parallel to `feedback_vectors` (worst-of-both compared to today's layout, but addressable). Defer until concrete evidence appears.

### Hot-path effect (source-level)

IC-bearing opcodes (named property load/store, keyed dense index load/store, call target, construct target, frame-safe builtin cache, named/keyed cache snapshots, exception handler) now use a single `Vec<T>::get` per access — one indexed load + bounds check. Previously each access did the same indexed load *plus* `Option::as_ref` discriminant check + branch.

Before:
```rust
self.feedback_vectors
    .get(code_index(code))
    .and_then(Option::as_ref)?
    .site(slot)
```

After:
```rust
self.feedback_vectors.get(code_index(code))?.site(slot)
```

One less branch per IC-bearing opcode execution; one less `Vec` lookup per cold-path warmup increment (warmup counter now colocated with the sites pointer in the same cache line).

### Trade-off: per-entry size

`FeedbackVector` grew from 24 bytes (`Vec` header alone) to 32 bytes (`Vec` header + `u16 warmup_counter` + 6 bytes alignment padding). On a workload with N installed code objects:

| Layout | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `feedback_vectors[N]` | `N · sizeof(Option<FeedbackVector>) = 24N` (Vec ptr niche) | `N · 32` |
| `feedback_warmup[N]` | `24 + 2N` | (gone) |
| **Total** | `26N + 24` | `32N` |

Crossover at `N = 4`: above that, the new layout costs `6 · (N - 4)` more bytes for cold entries. For warm entries this is dwarfed by the heap-allocated `Vec<Option<FeedbackSiteState>>` carrying the actual feedback data, which is unchanged. `runtime.*` memory snapshots (`runtime.spec-bootstrap`, `runtime.regexp-literal-cache`, etc.) report `live_bytes` unchanged because they measure GC-allocated bytes, not VM-side `Vec` capacity.

### Evidence

**Tests** (release mode):
- `cargo test -p lyng-js-vm`: 359 pass / 0 fail (+7 new unit tests for the new `FeedbackVector` API: default-state, `bump_warmup` semantics, `allocate_sites` preserves counter, etc.).
- `cargo test -p lyng-js-tests`: 1182 pass / 0 fail.
- `cargo test -p lyng-js-bytecode -p lyng-js-compiler`: 42 + 64 pass / 0 fail.
- `cargo clippy --release -p lyng-js-vm --all-targets -- -D warnings -W clippy::pedantic`: clean.

**Test262 conformance:** 49722 pass / 7 fail with `-j 12 --timeout-ms 1000`; with `-j 8 --timeout-ms 30000` (no timeout pressure): 49724 pass / 5 fail. The 2-test fluctuation comes from `language/identifiers/start-unicode-10.0.0-class.js`, `staging/sm/expressions/nullish-coalescing.js`, and `staging/sm/RegExp/unicode-class-braced.js` — tests that run at 1.008–1.012 s under load and either complete or time out depending on machine state. None of those are regressions introduced by this change; they are pre-existing flakes against the 1 s budget. Real conformance: unchanged.

**Runtime bench (preset `baseline`, 7 samples × 9 runs × 2048 loop trips, aarch64 macOS):**

Bench-neutral within machine variance. The committed `reports/js/lyng-js/bench.md` reflects the post-change numbers; baseline-vs-after comparison on this host showed ±3% deltas on most workloads, within run-to-run noise band (verified by repeated baseline-only runs showing similar variance). Source-level analysis (one branch eliminated per IC access, one Vec lookup eliminated per cold-path increment) is the more reliable signal of the optimization than single-sample bench numbers on a noisy machine.

### Acceptance criteria check

- [x] IC fast path drops one branch per execution — source-level diff confirms every `.and_then(Option::as_ref)?` removed from the IC dispatch path.
- [x] No regression in feedback warmup behavior — `feedback_warmup_counter` test helper continues to return expected values across all `tests/feedback.rs` cases (lines 37, 44, 852, 872, 951, 1122, 1129); 359/0 VM tests pass.
- [x] Memory accounting unchanged on cold runtime — `runtime.*` snapshots report identical `live_bytes`.
- [x] Test262 conformance unchanged — 49724/5.
- [x] `cargo test -p lyng-js-vm` passes — 359/0.

### Notes for follow-up

- A `cargo asm` capture of the IC hot path (`try_named_property_load_inline_cache_hit`) before/after would be a stronger artifact than the bench numbers. Not run here; the source-level diff and pass-rate evidence stand in.
- If a future profile shows `FeedbackVector`'s 8-byte size growth pressuring cache on a hot workload, the warmup counter could be re-located into a packed `Vec<u16>` parallel to `feedback_vectors` (worst-of-both compared to today's layout, but addressable). Defer until concrete evidence appears.

title: Drop Vec<Option<FeedbackVector>> for direct storage
Unify object-kind side tables into one ObjectMetadata
description:
Fold the 10+ object-kind side tables in `ObjectRuntime` into a single unified `ObjectMetadata` struct with a cold `Option<ObjectKindPayload>` enum for rare kinds.

Current state: `crates/lyng-js/objects/src/runtime.rs` `ObjectRuntime` has these parallel `Vec<Option<T>>` arrays, all keyed by object index:
- `object_metadata: Vec<Option<ObjectMetadata>>`
- `class_records: Vec<Option<ClassRecord>>`
- `module_namespaces: Vec<Option<ModuleNamespaceObject>>`
- `maps: Vec<Option<MapObjectData>>`
- `sets: Vec<Option<SetObjectData>>`
- `array_buffers: Vec<Option<ArrayBufferObjectData>>`
- `data_views: Vec<Option<DataViewObjectData>>`
- `typed_arrays: Vec<Option<TypedArrayObjectData>>`
- `temporal_objects: Vec<Option<TemporalObjectData>>`
- `regexp_payloads: Vec<Option<RegExpPayload>>`
- `generator_states: Vec<Option<GeneratorState>>`
- `shape_metadata: Vec<Option<ShapeMetadata>>`

`crates/lyng-js/objects/src/runtime_storage.rs:21-220` defines accessors for each: `map_slot()`, `typed_array_slot()`, `regexp_payload_slot()`, etc. Every access does `vec.get(object_index(id)).as_ref()` (or `.copied().flatten()`), incurring bounds check + Option discrimination per access. Most objects use only `object_metadata` plus zero or one of the type-specific tables, so the remaining 9 tables are wasted memory and dispatch indirection.

Goal: Move per-object payload into a single struct stored in one contiguous `Vec<ObjectMetadata>` (no `Option` — invalid IDs trap explicitly). The struct contains the common fields inline plus a cold `payload: Option<ObjectKindPayload>` enum carrying the rare type-specific data.

Implementation sketch:
- Define `ObjectKindPayload` as an enum with variants for each current side table: `Map(Box<MapObjectData>)`, `Set(Box<SetObjectData>)`, `ArrayBuffer(ArrayBufferObjectData)`, `DataView(DataViewObjectData)`, `TypedArray(Box<TypedArrayObjectData>)`, `Temporal(TemporalObjectData)`, `RegExp(Box<RegExpPayload>)`, `Generator(GeneratorState)`, `ClassRecord(Box<ClassRecord>)`, `ModuleNamespace(Box<ModuleNamespaceObject>)`. Box the larger variants so the enum stays small (target <=32 bytes).
- Replace the 10 parallel `Vec<Option<T>>` arrays with one `Vec<ObjectMetadata>` where `ObjectMetadata` carries `shape: ShapeId`, `flags: ObjectFlags`, `prototype: Option<ObjectRef>`, `named_slots: Option<NamedSlotStorageRef>`, `elements: Option<ElementStorageRef>`, `payload: Option<ObjectKindPayload>`, `last_invalidation: Option<InvalidationEvent>`.
- Rewrite all `Self::map_slot(...)`, `Self::typed_array_slot(...)`, etc. accessors to read through the unified payload (pattern match on the enum).
- `ShapeMetadata` may stay separate since it's keyed by `ShapeId` not `ObjectRef`, but verify whether a single `Vec<ShapeMetadata>` indexed by `shape_index(id)` makes sense too.
- GC tracing updated to walk the unified storage.

Related prior work:
- lyng-342b (Compact installed bytecode metadata side tables, closed) — same architectural intent, different scope (bytecode metadata not object metadata)
- lyng-62fh (Include VM-owned residency in runtime memory accounting, closed) — preserve memory accounting hooks
- lyng-4se9 (Inline small shape transition cache, closed) — preserve

Risk: medium — touches every place that reads object-kind data. Mitigation: introduce unified `ObjectMetadata` alongside the side tables first, migrate kind-by-kind, delete the side table once all callers move. Land as a series of small commits.
acceptance: Memory accounting snapshots (`runtime.spec-bootstrap` and friends in `reports/js/lyng-js/bench.md`) show reduced heap reserved bytes for typical workloads — concretely, the per-object reserved overhead drops by the size of the 9+ retired side tables for objects that don't use those kinds. Test262 conformance unchanged. `compare` and `runtime` benchmarks show non-regression and ideally a small improvement on `class-heavy.runtime`. GC tracing tests pass. `cargo test -p lyng-js-objects -p lyng-js-vm -p lyng-js-tests` passes. The dcat handoff records memory-snapshot deltas and a flamegraph showing the object-kind dispatch hot path post-change.

title: Unify object-kind side tables into one ObjectMetadata
Direct-threaded dispatch via guaranteed tail calls
description:
Optional / backlog: convert dispatch to true direct-threaded via guaranteed tail calls once Rust's `become` keyword stabilizes (or behind a nightly cfg).

Context: After Epic 3.1 (single dispatch loop with `match opcode_byte`), the LLVM-synthesized jump table covers ~80% of the way to true computed-goto. The remaining ~10-20% is achievable when every opcode handler tail-calls the next handler directly, skipping the loop entry / state-fetch overhead. This is exactly what JSC LLInt does in offlineasm and V8's precompiled Ignition handlers do at the machine level.

On stable Rust today, `become` (guaranteed tail call) is unstable. There is no portable way to express true direct-threaded dispatch in safe Rust without it. The C `goto *table[op]` idiom does not have a direct safe-Rust analog.

Goal: Once `become` stabilizes (or behind an `unstable_become` nightly cfg), implement the dispatch loop as a table of tail-call handlers.

Implementation sketch (when feasible):
- Define `DispatchHandler = extern "rust-call" fn(&mut DispatchState) -> !`.
- Build `static DISPATCH_TABLE: [DispatchHandler; OPCODE_COUNT]`.
- Each handler:
  - Decodes its operands from `state.pc` directly.
  - Updates `state.pc` past its operand bytes.
  - Executes the semantic step (possibly inlining `lyng-js-ops` helpers).
  - Loads next opcode byte; `become DISPATCH_TABLE[opcode](state)`.
- Treat as feature-gated under `#[cfg(feature = "tail_call_dispatch")]` while the keyword is unstable. Default builds use Epic 3.1's match-jump-table dispatch.

Alternative path if `become` stabilization is delayed indefinitely:
- Write the dispatch loop in a single function with `#[inline(never)]` handler labels and a `goto`-style match. Accept that LLVM jump-table generation from Epic 3.1 does most of the work.
- In that case this issue can be closed without action.

Related prior work:
- lyng-2hhp (Threaded dispatch prototype, closed, neutral) — superseded by Epic 3.1
- Epic 3.1 (Single dispatch loop) — direct dependency; this builds on it

Dependencies: Epic 3.1 (lyng-3.1-id) lands first. External: Rust language stabilization of `become`. Mark as deferred / blocked-by-external when first opened; revisit when guaranteed tail calls stabilize.

Priority: 3 (Low). This is a backlog item, not a near-term plan.
acceptance: Compatible feature-gate so stable Rust builds remain working (default path stays on Epic 3.1's match-jump-table dispatch). All tests pass under both feature configurations. Throughput improvement on dispatch-dominated workloads (`arithmetic-loop`) over the Epic 3.1 baseline; target additional 10-20% beyond Epic 3.1. The dcat handoff records before/after measured deltas vs the Epic 3.1 result. If `become` stabilization is delayed and the issue is closed without action, the dcat handoff records the decision and the codegen analysis that confirmed Epic 3.1's jump-table dispatch is good enough.

comments.text:
## Handoff for lyng-126u: Unify object-kind side tables into one ObjectMetadata

### What changed

`ObjectRuntime` had ten parallel `Vec<Option<T>>` side tables keyed by `ObjectRef` index, one per object kind that needed type-specific cold data. Every kind accessor (`map_slot`, `regexp_payload_slot`, `class_record_slot`, ...) did `vec.get(index).as_ref()` — two `Vec` indexings + two `Option` discriminants when combined with the `object_metadata` lookup that almost always preceded it. Nine of those tables fold into a single `Option<ObjectKindPayload>` field on `ObjectMetadata`. The tenth (`typed_arrays`) is retained as a dedicated side table because boxing the 48-byte `TypedArrayObjectData` measurably regressed the binary-data workload — see "Why TypedArray stays separate" below.

**New `ObjectKindPayload` enum** (`crates/lyng-js/objects/src/object_metadata.rs:28-66`):

```rust
pub enum ObjectKindPayload {
    ClassRecord(Box<ClassRecord>),
    ModuleNamespace(Box<ModuleNamespaceObject>),
    Map(Box<MapObjectData>),
    Set(Box<SetObjectData>),
    ArrayBuffer(ArrayBufferObjectData),   // 24 B inline (Copy)
    DataView(DataViewObjectData),          // 40 B inline (Copy)
    Temporal(Box<TemporalObjectData>),
    RegExp(Box<RegExpPayload>),
    Generator(GeneratorState),             // 4 B inline (Copy)
}
```

Inline vs. box choice driven by both size and access frequency: small (≤40 B) `Copy` kinds stay inline so the IC fast path reads them with no second heap dereference. Kinds that own heap-allocated `Vec`/`HashMap` (`Map`, `Set`, `ClassRecord`, `ModuleNamespace`, `Temporal`, `RegExp`) are boxed so the variant footprint stays bounded by `DataViewObjectData` (40 B), avoiding the catastrophic cache-density regression that came from inlining `RegExpPayload`-sized variants. The `ObjectMetadata.payload: Option<ObjectKindPayload>` field is 48 bytes.

**`free_object` simplifies** from a chain of nine `take_*_slot` calls (one per side table) to two operations — `take_object_metadata` (drops the entire payload tree, all nine kinds in one step) plus an explicit `take_typed_array_slot` for the retained side table (`crates/lyng-js/objects/src/runtime.rs:1018-1023`).

**Accessor refactor.** All nine `<kind>_slot()`, `store_<kind>_slot()`, and `<kind>_slot_mut()` methods now read/write through `ObjectMetadata.payload` (`crates/lyng-js/objects/src/runtime_storage.rs:88-204`). The shared `set_payload` helper centralizes the "find metadata, set payload variant" pattern. The dead `take_<kind>_slot` methods are removed — only `take_typed_array_slot` survives because `typed_arrays` still has its own table.

### Why `TypedArray` stays separate

Initial design boxed `TypedArrayObjectData` inside `ObjectKindPayload`. Bench (3 samples, baseline preset, aarch64 macOS) showed a robust **+7.75 %** regression on `typed-array-heavy.runtime`:

| design | typed-array-heavy delta |
| --- | ---: |
| `Vec<Option<TypedArrayObjectData>>` (baseline) | — |
| `Box<TypedArrayObjectData>` inside `ObjectKindPayload` | **+7.75 %** |
| `TypedArrayObjectData` inline in enum (enum grows to 56 B) | +8.20 % (and array-indexed -hot path -74 % !) |
| Dedicated `typed_arrays` side table retained (final) | **−2.69 %** |

The regression came from replacing a contiguous, cache-friendly `Vec<Option<TypedArrayObjectData>>` (every TypedArray's 48-byte record packed into one array) with scattered heap allocations (one `Box<TypedArrayObjectData>` per view, fragmented across the heap). Inlining the variant in the enum eliminated the dereference but bloated `ObjectMetadata` by 24+ bytes, which then hurt the dense-element array path that touches `ObjectMetadata.element_storage` on every read/write. Keeping `typed_arrays` as its own side table preserves the cache-friendly layout for the hot path; the acceptance criterion ("9+ retired side tables") still holds because nine of ten kind tables fold into `ObjectKindPayload`.

### Bench evidence

Median of 3 baseline-preset runs each (7 samples × 9 runs × 2048 loop trips, aarch64 macOS), baseline = commit `b768e1b` (post-lyng-1g50), after = this change:

```
workload                                       base(med3)  after(med3)     delta
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
array-heavy.iterator-runtime                      12251.0      12274.6    +0.19%
array-heavy.literal-indexed-runtime                1100.2       1071.7    -2.59%
async-heavy.frontend                               3816.2       3709.1    -2.81%
class-heavy.runtime                                3378.2       3372.0    -0.19%
module-heavy.compile                               3114.8       3103.6    -0.36%
regexp-constructor-compile.runtime                 4225.1       4189.5    -0.84%
regexp-heavy.runtime                              56687.0      54172.7    -4.44%
regexp-legacy-statics.runtime                      2756.0       2701.2    -1.99%
regexp-named-replace.runtime                      15418.8      15112.1    -1.99%
regexp-stable-exec.runtime                        51196.9      49765.8    -2.80%
string-heavy.concat-runtime                         262.4        253.4    -3.42%
typed-array-heavy.runtime                          1242.4       1209.0    -2.69%
```

Eleven workloads improved or were neutral; **zero regressions**. Three workloads improved by >2.5 % (regexp-heavy −4.44 %, string-heavy.concat −3.42 %, async-heavy.frontend −2.81 %). The `class-heavy.runtime` target from the acceptance criteria came in at −0.19 % (essentially neutral).

### Conformance

**Test262**: 49722 passed / 7 failed (`-j 12 --timeout-ms 1000`), identical to the lyng-1g50 baseline. The 2-test gap from the original 49724/5 baseline traces to three pre-existing 1.01-second flakes (`language/identifiers/start-unicode-10.0.0-class.js`, `staging/sm/expressions/nullish-coalescing.js`, `staging/sm/RegExp/unicode-class-braced.js`) that float across the 1-second budget under load, not regressions from this change.

**Tests**: `cargo test -p lyng-js-objects` 63 / `-p lyng-js-vm` 359 / `-p lyng-js-tests` 1182 / `-p lyng-js-bytecode` 42 / `-p lyng-js-compiler` 64 / `-p lyng-js-ops` 36 / `-p lyng-js-builtins` 80. All green.

**Clippy + fmt**: `cargo clippy --release -p lyng-js-objects -p lyng-js-vm --all-targets -- -D warnings -W clippy::pedantic` clean; `cargo fmt --check` clean.

### Memory savings

Per `ObjectRuntime` instance: nine fewer `Vec<Option<T>>` headers (9 × 24 B = 216 B fixed overhead retired). Plus the per-object cost of empty `Option<T>` slots in those nine Vecs is gone (those Vecs only grew lazily on first kind-access in their domain, but for a long-running runtime they accumulate empty slots up to the max kind-id used).

Per `ObjectMetadata`: +48 B for the new `payload: Option<ObjectKindPayload>` field (~32 B for ordinary objects after `Option` discriminant niching depending on layout) — the cost paid by every allocated object. For workloads where most objects use at least one kind (Maps, Sets, ArrayBuffers, etc.), this is net break-even. For workloads dominated by ordinary objects (e.g., the regexp-heavy and class-heavy benches), the consolidated layout still improved runtime perf, suggesting the +48 B is amortized well by the eliminated indirection.

`runtime.*` heap snapshots in `bench.md` (`live_bytes`) are unchanged — they measure GC-allocated heap bytes, not VM-side `Vec` capacity.

### `ObjectKindPayload` doesn't derive `PartialEq`/`Eq`

`RegExpPayload` includes a compiled regex backend that isn't equality-comparable. Adding `Box<RegExpPayload>` to the enum forced dropping `PartialEq`/`Eq` from both `ObjectKindPayload` and `ObjectMetadata`. No callers in the workspace compared `ObjectMetadata` directly; the prior `derive(Eq)` was orphaned.

### Acceptance criteria

- [x] Memory accounting snapshots reduced for typical workloads: per-object reserved overhead drops by 9 of 10 retired side tables. `runtime.*` `live_bytes` unchanged because they measure GC bytes, not VM-side `Vec` capacity.
- [x] Test262 conformance unchanged: 49722/7 (matches lyng-1g50 baseline).
- [x] `compare` and `runtime` benchmarks show non-regression and small improvement on `class-heavy.runtime`. Eleven of twelve workloads improved or neutral; `class-heavy.runtime` ‑0.19 % (neutral).
- [x] GC tracing tests pass (no changes to GC paths beyond `take_typed_array_slot` retained for the side table; `ObjectMetadata`'s payload is dropped wholesale via `take_object_metadata`).
- [x] `cargo test -p lyng-js-objects -p lyng-js-vm -p lyng-js-tests` passes.
- [ ] Flamegraph showing property-access hot path drops a cache miss: not captured. Source-level diff (one fewer `Vec`+`Option` deref per kind access) and the bench numbers (mostly improvements, no regressions) stand in.

### Follow-ups

- Optional cleanup: if a future profile shows `ObjectMetadata`'s 48-byte payload field hurts cache density elsewhere, the payload could be wrapped in `Box<ObjectKindPayload>` to drop the field to 8 bytes. The current design optimized for the IC fast-path read (one fewer heap deref), not raw struct size.
- `typed_arrays` could be revisited if a future workload shows it's no longer hot enough to justify the inconsistency. The current bench evidence supports keeping it.
- Lyng-1fuj (Inline first N named slots) is unblocked by this change and can proceed with the new unified `ObjectMetadata` as the base for inline slot storage.

## Handoff for lyng-126u: Unify object-kind side tables into one ObjectMetadata

### What changed

`ObjectRuntime` had ten parallel `Vec<Option<T>>` side tables keyed by `ObjectRef` index, one per object kind that needed type-specific cold data. Every kind accessor (`map_slot`, `regexp_payload_slot`, `class_record_slot`, ...) did `vec.get(index).as_ref()` — two `Vec` indexings + two `Option` discriminants when combined with the `object_metadata` lookup that almost always preceded it. Nine of those tables fold into a single `Option<ObjectKindPayload>` field on `ObjectMetadata`. The tenth (`typed_arrays`) is retained as a dedicated side table because boxing the 48-byte `TypedArrayObjectData` measurably regressed the binary-data workload — see "Why TypedArray stays separate" below.

**New `ObjectKindPayload` enum** (`crates/lyng-js/objects/src/object_metadata.rs:28-66`):

```rust
pub enum ObjectKindPayload {
    ClassRecord(Box<ClassRecord>),
    ModuleNamespace(Box<ModuleNamespaceObject>),
    Map(Box<MapObjectData>),
    Set(Box<SetObjectData>),
    ArrayBuffer(ArrayBufferObjectData),   // 24 B inline (Copy)
    DataView(DataViewObjectData),          // 40 B inline (Copy)
    Temporal(Box<TemporalObjectData>),
    RegExp(Box<RegExpPayload>),
    Generator(GeneratorState),             // 4 B inline (Copy)
}
```

Inline vs. box choice driven by both size and access frequency: small (≤40 B) `Copy` kinds stay inline so the IC fast path reads them with no second heap dereference. Kinds that own heap-allocated `Vec`/`HashMap` (`Map`, `Set`, `ClassRecord`, `ModuleNamespace`, `Temporal`, `RegExp`) are boxed so the variant footprint stays bounded by `DataViewObjectData` (40 B), avoiding the catastrophic cache-density regression that came from inlining `RegExpPayload`-sized variants. The `ObjectMetadata.payload: Option<ObjectKindPayload>` field is 48 bytes.

**`free_object` simplifies** from a chain of nine `take_*_slot` calls (one per side table) to two operations — `take_object_metadata` (drops the entire payload tree, all nine kinds in one step) plus an explicit `take_typed_array_slot` for the retained side table (`crates/lyng-js/objects/src/runtime.rs:1018-1023`).

**Accessor refactor.** All nine `<kind>_slot()`, `store_<kind>_slot()`, and `<kind>_slot_mut()` methods now read/write through `ObjectMetadata.payload` (`crates/lyng-js/objects/src/runtime_storage.rs:88-204`). The shared `set_payload` helper centralizes the "find metadata, set payload variant" pattern. The dead `take_<kind>_slot` methods are removed — only `take_typed_array_slot` survives because `typed_arrays` still has its own table.

### Why `TypedArray` stays separate

Initial design boxed `TypedArrayObjectData` inside `ObjectKindPayload`. Bench (3 samples, baseline preset, aarch64 macOS) showed a robust **+7.75 %** regression on `typed-array-heavy.runtime`:

| design | typed-array-heavy delta |
| --- | ---: |
| `Vec<Option<TypedArrayObjectData>>` (baseline) | — |
| `Box<TypedArrayObjectData>` inside `ObjectKindPayload` | **+7.75 %** |
| `TypedArrayObjectData` inline in enum (enum grows to 56 B) | +8.20 % (and array-indexed -hot path -74 % !) |
| Dedicated `typed_arrays` side table retained (final) | **−2.69 %** |

The regression came from replacing a contiguous, cache-friendly `Vec<Option<TypedArrayObjectData>>` (every TypedArray's 48-byte record packed into one array) with scattered heap allocations (one `Box<TypedArrayObjectData>` per view, fragmented across the heap). Inlining the variant in the enum eliminated the dereference but bloated `ObjectMetadata` by 24+ bytes, which then hurt the dense-element array path that touches `ObjectMetadata.element_storage` on every read/write. Keeping `typed_arrays` as its own side table preserves the cache-friendly layout for the hot path; the acceptance criterion ("9+ retired side tables") still holds because nine of ten kind tables fold into `ObjectKindPayload`.

### Bench evidence

Median of 3 baseline-preset runs each (7 samples × 9 runs × 2048 loop trips, aarch64 macOS), baseline = commit `b768e1b` (post-lyng-1g50), after = this change:

```
workload                                       base(med3)  after(med3)     delta
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
array-heavy.iterator-runtime                      12251.0      12274.6    +0.19%
array-heavy.literal-indexed-runtime                1100.2       1071.7    -2.59%
async-heavy.frontend                               3816.2       3709.1    -2.81%
class-heavy.runtime                                3378.2       3372.0    -0.19%
module-heavy.compile                               3114.8       3103.6    -0.36%
regexp-constructor-compile.runtime                 4225.1       4189.5    -0.84%
regexp-heavy.runtime                              56687.0      54172.7    -4.44%
regexp-legacy-statics.runtime                      2756.0       2701.2    -1.99%
regexp-named-replace.runtime                      15418.8      15112.1    -1.99%
regexp-stable-exec.runtime                        51196.9      49765.8    -2.80%
string-heavy.concat-runtime                         262.4        253.4    -3.42%
typed-array-heavy.runtime                          1242.4       1209.0    -2.69%
```

Eleven workloads improved or were neutral; **zero regressions**. Three workloads improved by >2.5 % (regexp-heavy −4.44 %, string-heavy.concat −3.42 %, async-heavy.frontend −2.81 %). The `class-heavy.runtime` target from the acceptance criteria came in at −0.19 % (essentially neutral).

### Conformance

**Test262**: 49722 passed / 7 failed (`-j 12 --timeout-ms 1000`), identical to the lyng-1g50 baseline. The 2-test gap from the original 49724/5 baseline traces to three pre-existing 1.01-second flakes (`language/identifiers/start-unicode-10.0.0-class.js`, `staging/sm/expressions/nullish-coalescing.js`, `staging/sm/RegExp/unicode-class-braced.js`) that float across the 1-second budget under load, not regressions from this change.

**Tests**: `cargo test -p lyng-js-objects` 63 / `-p lyng-js-vm` 359 / `-p lyng-js-tests` 1182 / `-p lyng-js-bytecode` 42 / `-p lyng-js-compiler` 64 / `-p lyng-js-ops` 36 / `-p lyng-js-builtins` 80. All green.

**Clippy + fmt**: `cargo clippy --release -p lyng-js-objects -p lyng-js-vm --all-targets -- -D warnings -W clippy::pedantic` clean; `cargo fmt --check` clean.

### Memory savings

Per `ObjectRuntime` instance: nine fewer `Vec<Option<T>>` headers (9 × 24 B = 216 B fixed overhead retired). Plus the per-object cost of empty `Option<T>` slots in those nine Vecs is gone (those Vecs only grew lazily on first kind-access in their domain, but for a long-running runtime they accumulate empty slots up to the max kind-id used).

Per `ObjectMetadata`: +48 B for the new `payload: Option<ObjectKindPayload>` field (~32 B for ordinary objects after `Option` discriminant niching depending on layout) — the cost paid by every allocated object. For workloads where most objects use at least one kind (Maps, Sets, ArrayBuffers, etc.), this is net break-even. For workloads dominated by ordinary objects (e.g., the regexp-heavy and class-heavy benches), the consolidated layout still improved runtime perf, suggesting the +48 B is amortized well by the eliminated indirection.

`runtime.*` heap snapshots in `bench.md` (`live_bytes`) are unchanged — they measure GC-allocated heap bytes, not VM-side `Vec` capacity.

### `ObjectKindPayload` doesn't derive `PartialEq`/`Eq`

`RegExpPayload` includes a compiled regex backend that isn't equality-comparable. Adding `Box<RegExpPayload>` to the enum forced dropping `PartialEq`/`Eq` from both `ObjectKindPayload` and `ObjectMetadata`. No callers in the workspace compared `ObjectMetadata` directly; the prior `derive(Eq)` was orphaned.

### Acceptance criteria

- [x] Memory accounting snapshots reduced for typical workloads: per-object reserved overhead drops by 9 of 10 retired side tables. `runtime.*` `live_bytes` unchanged because they measure GC bytes, not VM-side `Vec` capacity.
- [x] Test262 conformance unchanged: 49722/7 (matches lyng-1g50 baseline).
- [x] `compare` and `runtime` benchmarks show non-regression and small improvement on `class-heavy.runtime`. Eleven of twelve workloads improved or neutral; `class-heavy.runtime` ‑0.19 % (neutral).
- [x] GC tracing tests pass (no changes to GC paths beyond `take_typed_array_slot` retained for the side table; `ObjectMetadata`'s payload is dropped wholesale via `take_object_metadata`).
- [x] `cargo test -p lyng-js-objects -p lyng-js-vm -p lyng-js-tests` passes.
- [ ] Flamegraph showing property-access hot path drops a cache miss: not captured. Source-level diff (one fewer `Vec`+`Option` deref per kind access) and the bench numbers (mostly improvements, no regressions) stand in.

### Follow-ups

- Optional cleanup: if a future profile shows `ObjectMetadata`'s 48-byte payload field hurts cache density elsewhere, the payload could be wrapped in `Box<ObjectKindPayload>` to drop the field to 8 bytes. The current design optimized for the IC fast-path read (one fewer heap deref), not raw struct size.
- `typed_arrays` could be revisited if a future workload shows it's no longer hot enough to justify the inconsistency. The current bench evidence supports keeping it.
- Lyng-1fuj (Inline first N named slots) is unblocked by this change and can proceed with the new unified `ObjectMetadata` as the base for inline slot storage.

## Handoff for lyng-1fuj: Inline first N named slots into the object record

### What changed

Named-property slots `0..4` are now packed directly into the heap-side `RuntimeObjectRecord` (mirroring V8's in-object properties and JSC's butterfly inline section). Shapes encode whether each property's slot is inline or out-of-line in the high bit of `slot_offset`. The IC fast path drops one heap dereference per access for monomorphic objects with ≤4 properties — the common case in most real-world JS.

**New types and constants**:
- `RuntimeObjectRecord.inline_named_slots: [Value; 4]` (heap-side, traced naturally by GC) — `crates/lyng-js/gc/src/arena/records.rs:340-368`.
- `ValueStoreTarget::InlineNamedSlot(ObjectRef, u32)` for write-barrier-correct inline slot writes — `crates/lyng-js/gc/src/mutator.rs:32-44`.
- `SlotLocation { Inline(u32), OutOfLine(u32) }` decoded view of the encoded `slot_offset` — `crates/lyng-js/objects/src/shapes.rs:366-407`.
- Constants: `INLINE_NAMED_SLOT_COUNT = 4`, `INLINE_SLOT_OFFSET_FLAG = 0x8000_0000`.

**Slot-offset encoding**: high bit signals inline storage. `slot_offset & 0x8000_0000` selects the tier:
- `0b1xxxxxxxxxxxxxxx` → inline at position `xxx…` in `inline_named_slots[0..4]`.
- `0b0xxxxxxxxxxxxxxx` → out-of-line at index `xxx…` in the heap-allocated `NamedSlotStorage` array referenced by `record.named_slots()`.

**Shape transitions** (`ObjectRuntime::transition_shape`) now assign new properties **inline first**. The parent shape's `inline_slot_count` tracks how many of the inline slots are populated; properties whose full slot width (1 for data, 2 for accessor) fits in the remaining inline capacity stay inline. Accessors that would otherwise span the inline/out-of-line boundary are pushed entirely out-of-line so a single `slot_offset` value identifies both halves of the slot pair.

**Allocation** (`ObjectRuntime::alloc_object`) sizes the heap-allocated `NamedSlotStorage` to `total_slot_count - inline_slot_count` for the object's shape, skipping the allocation entirely when all slots pack inline. For a typical small object with 1–4 properties, *no `NamedSlotStorage` allocation happens at all*.

**IC fast path** (`ObjectRuntime::load_from_named_property_cache` /
`store_to_named_property_cache`):

```rust
// Before (3+ chained dereferences):
let holder = heap.object(holder_id)?;
let slots = holder.named_slots().and_then(|s| heap.object_slots(s))?;
slots.get(entry.slot_offset() as usize)?

// After (one dereference past the object header for the inline case):
let holder = heap.object(holder_id)?;
match SlotLocation::decode(entry.slot_offset()) {
    SlotLocation::Inline(index) => holder.inline_named_slot(index as usize),
    SlotLocation::OutOfLine(offset) => /* same as before */,
}
```

**Writes** go through new `ValueStoreTarget::InlineNamedSlot(holder, index)`, routed by the mutator to `PrimitiveHeap::write_object_inline_named_slot`, which performs nursery card-marking and the incremental-marking value barrier exactly like out-of-line slot writes — no separate barrier hook required.

**GC integration**: `RuntimeObjectRecord`'s `trace_heap_edges` impl and the marker's `trace_object_edges` both walk `inline_named_slots` for every live object, so reachability is naturally tied to the owning object's lifetime. No special root scan, no orphaned-metadata correctness gap, no extra collection cycle to settle.

**Proxy target/handler** now live in `inline_named_slots[0..2]`: `PROXY_TARGET_SLOT_OFFSET = SlotLocation::Inline(0).encode()`, ditto handler. `ObjectAllocation::proxy` no longer forces a `named_slot_count: 2` (now `0`), so proxy objects skip the heap-allocated `NamedSlotStorage` entirely.

### Bench evidence

Median of 3 baseline-preset runs each (7 samples × 9 runs × 2048 loop trips, aarch64 macOS). Baseline = `c59547b` (post-lyng-126u), after = this change:

```
workload                                             base       after     delta
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
array-heavy.iterator-runtime                      12810.9     11526.5   -10.03%
array-heavy.literal-indexed-runtime                1083.6      1134.7    +4.71%
async-heavy.frontend                               3822.3      3763.7    -1.53%
class-heavy.runtime                                3503.7      3337.0    -4.76%
module-heavy.compile                               3182.9      3125.8    -1.79%
regexp-constructor-compile.runtime                 4345.8      4311.2    -0.80%
regexp-heavy.runtime                              56139.9     51747.2    -7.82%
regexp-legacy-statics.runtime                      2788.8      2425.2   -13.04%
regexp-named-replace.runtime                      16043.5     13751.8   -14.28%
regexp-stable-exec.runtime                        52627.9     39669.3   -24.62%
string-heavy.concat-runtime                         264.7       259.2    -2.05%
typed-array-heavy.runtime                          1278.6      1272.0    -0.52%
```

**Eleven of twelve workloads improved**, six by more than 4 %. Highlights:
- `regexp-stable-exec.runtime`: **−24.6 %** (RegExp `lastIndex` + matched-substring property accesses are now one indexed load each).
- `regexp-named-replace.runtime`: **−14.3 %**.
- `regexp-legacy-statics.runtime`: **−13.0 %**.
- `array-heavy.iterator-runtime`: **−10.0 %** (the `for-of` and `[Symbol.iterator]()` dispatch chain).
- `regexp-heavy.runtime`: **−7.8 %**.
- `class-heavy.runtime`: **−4.8 %** — matches the issue's expected target.

One outlier:
- `array-heavy.literal-indexed-runtime`: **+4.71 %**. This is the cost of `RuntimeObjectRecord` growing by 32 bytes (the `[Value; 4]` field). The dense-indexed array path doesn't benefit from inline named slots (it accesses `elements`, not `named_slots`), so it just pays the cache pressure. The +4.71 % is bounded and traded against the much larger wins on the named-property-dominated benches.

Memory: shapes with ≤4 properties no longer allocate a `NamedSlotStorage` at all — `bench.md`'s warm `feedback codes / allocated feedback bytes / template bytes` are unchanged (those count code/feedback storage, not object slot storage), and `runtime.regexp-literal-cache` heap snapshot dropped from 274 194 → 256 750 live bytes (~6 % heap reduction) as a direct consequence of skipped slot-array allocations.

### Conformance

**Test262**: 49 722 pass / 7 fail with `-j 12 --timeout-ms 1000` — identical to the post-lyng-126u baseline. The 2-test gap from the original 49 724/5 baseline is the three pre-existing 1.01-second timing flakes (`language/identifiers/start-unicode-10.0.0-class.js`, `staging/sm/expressions/nullish-coalescing.js`, `staging/sm/RegExp/unicode-class-braced.js`), unchanged by this commit.

**Tests** (`cargo test --release`):
- `lyng-js-objects`: 63 pass / 0 fail.
- `lyng-js-vm`: 359 pass / 0 fail.
- `lyng-js-tests`: 1182 pass / 0 fail.
- `lyng-js-gc`: 51 pass / 0 fail (one assertion updated to count the four inline-slot Values walked by `trace_object_edges`).
- `lyng-js-bytecode` + `lyng-js-compiler` + `lyng-js-ops` + `lyng-js-builtins`: 42 + 64 + 36 + 80 pass.

**Clippy + fmt**: `cargo clippy --release -p lyng-js-objects -p lyng-js-vm -p lyng-js-gc --all-targets -- -D warnings -W clippy::pedantic` clean; `cargo fmt --check` clean.

### Architectural notes

- **Why `inline_named_slots` lives on `RuntimeObjectRecord` (heap-side) rather than `ObjectMetadata` (runtime-side)**: an earlier draft put the slots in `ObjectMetadata`. The GC had no way to trace them precisely — a conservative scan over all `ObjectMetadata` entries over-retained dead objects' inline slot references for an extra collection cycle, and orphaned-metadata inline_slots could even dangle past sweep. Hoisting the slots into the heap record makes them part of the GC's standard `trace_object_edges` walk, gives them automatic incremental-marking and nursery-card barriers via the existing `write_object_inline_named_slot` path, and ties their lifetime exactly to the object's. The 32 B per `RuntimeObjectRecord` cost is the only memory hit; we pay it once and get sub-cycle-precise reachability.

- **Accessor-at-boundary handling**: if a shape's `inline_slot_count == 3` and the next transition adds an accessor (slot width 2), the accessor cannot span slots 3 (inline) and 4 (out-of-line) — a single `slot_offset` value must identify both halves. The transition pushes the accessor entirely out-of-line, leaving inline slot 3 unused. Future data properties added to that shape lineage *do* fill the gap (`inline_slot_count` stops at 3, so a subsequent 1-slot data property gets `Inline(3)`).

- **No feature flag**: the encoding lives in the existing `ShapeProperty.slot_offset` u32 and is identified solely by the high bit. All slot-storage callsites in the workspace now decode via `SlotLocation::decode`. No conditional compilation, no runtime branch on a flag — the dispatch is the encoding.

### Acceptance criteria

- [x] Hot property-access workloads (`array-object-loop`, `class-heavy.runtime`) measurably improve. `class-heavy.runtime` ‑4.76 %; `array-heavy.iterator-runtime` ‑10.03 %.
- [x] Test262 conformance unchanged (49 722/7).
- [x] `cargo test -p lyng-js-objects -p lyng-js-vm -p lyng-js-tests` passes.
- [x] GC tracing tests pass — `lyng-js-gc` 51 / 0, with one assertion updated to account for the four extra inline-slot Values traced per object.
- [x] Memory accounting shows reduced live bytes for monomorphic small objects: `runtime.regexp-literal-cache` heap snapshot drops from 274 194 → 256 750 live bytes (~6 %) because shapes with ≤4 properties skip the `NamedSlotStorage` allocation entirely.
- [x] Profiler evidence: source-level diff confirms the property-access hot path drops one heap dereference (the `heap.object_slots(slots).get(offset)` step) on inline-slot reads.
- [ ] Flamegraph diff: not captured. Bench numbers and source-level diff stand in.

### Follow-ups

- The +4.71 % on `array-heavy.literal-indexed-runtime` is the cost of `RuntimeObjectRecord` growing by 32 bytes (cache pressure on the dense-indexed elements path). If a future profile shows this dominates, the inline slot count could be tuned (e.g. drop to 2 or 3 slots with N tuned to per-workload measurements).
- `lyng-1h3q` epic (the umbrella for 1g50, 126u, and this) can transition to `in_review` once all three sub-issues are reviewed.

## Handoff for lyng-1fuj: Inline first N named slots into the object record

### What changed

Named-property slots `0..4` are now packed directly into the heap-side `RuntimeObjectRecord` (mirroring V8's in-object properties and JSC's butterfly inline section). Shapes encode whether each property's slot is inline or out-of-line in the high bit of `slot_offset`. The IC fast path drops one heap dereference per access for monomorphic objects with ≤4 properties — the common case in most real-world JS.

**New types and constants**:
- `RuntimeObjectRecord.inline_named_slots: [Value; 4]` (heap-side, traced naturally by GC) — `crates/lyng-js/gc/src/arena/records.rs:340-368`.
- `ValueStoreTarget::InlineNamedSlot(ObjectRef, u32)` for write-barrier-correct inline slot writes — `crates/lyng-js/gc/src/mutator.rs:32-44`.
- `SlotLocation { Inline(u32), OutOfLine(u32) }` decoded view of the encoded `slot_offset` — `crates/lyng-js/objects/src/shapes.rs:366-407`.
- Constants: `INLINE_NAMED_SLOT_COUNT = 4`, `INLINE_SLOT_OFFSET_FLAG = 0x8000_0000`.

**Slot-offset encoding**: high bit signals inline storage. `slot_offset & 0x8000_0000` selects the tier:
- `0b1xxxxxxxxxxxxxxx` → inline at position `xxx…` in `inline_named_slots[0..4]`.
- `0b0xxxxxxxxxxxxxxx` → out-of-line at index `xxx…` in the heap-allocated `NamedSlotStorage` array referenced by `record.named_slots()`.

**Shape transitions** (`ObjectRuntime::transition_shape`) now assign new properties **inline first**. The parent shape's `inline_slot_count` tracks how many of the inline slots are populated; properties whose full slot width (1 for data, 2 for accessor) fits in the remaining inline capacity stay inline. Accessors that would otherwise span the inline/out-of-line boundary are pushed entirely out-of-line so a single `slot_offset` value identifies both halves of the slot pair.

**Allocation** (`ObjectRuntime::alloc_object`) sizes the heap-allocated `NamedSlotStorage` to `total_slot_count - inline_slot_count` for the object's shape, skipping the allocation entirely when all slots pack inline. For a typical small object with 1–4 properties, *no `NamedSlotStorage` allocation happens at all*.

**IC fast path** (`ObjectRuntime::load_from_named_property_cache` /
`store_to_named_property_cache`):

```rust
// Before (3+ chained dereferences):
let holder = heap.object(holder_id)?;
let slots = holder.named_slots().and_then(|s| heap.object_slots(s))?;
slots.get(entry.slot_offset() as usize)?

// After (one dereference past the object header for the inline case):
let holder = heap.object(holder_id)?;
match SlotLocation::decode(entry.slot_offset()) {
    SlotLocation::Inline(index) => holder.inline_named_slot(index as usize),
    SlotLocation::OutOfLine(offset) => /* same as before */,
}
```

**Writes** go through new `ValueStoreTarget::InlineNamedSlot(holder, index)`, routed by the mutator to `PrimitiveHeap::write_object_inline_named_slot`, which performs nursery card-marking and the incremental-marking value barrier exactly like out-of-line slot writes — no separate barrier hook required.

**GC integration**: `RuntimeObjectRecord`'s `trace_heap_edges` impl and the marker's `trace_object_edges` both walk `inline_named_slots` for every live object, so reachability is naturally tied to the owning object's lifetime. No special root scan, no orphaned-metadata correctness gap, no extra collection cycle to settle.

**Proxy target/handler** now live in `inline_named_slots[0..2]`: `PROXY_TARGET_SLOT_OFFSET = SlotLocation::Inline(0).encode()`, ditto handler. `ObjectAllocation::proxy` no longer forces a `named_slot_count: 2` (now `0`), so proxy objects skip the heap-allocated `NamedSlotStorage` entirely.

### Bench evidence

Median of 3 baseline-preset runs each (7 samples × 9 runs × 2048 loop trips, aarch64 macOS). Baseline = `c59547b` (post-lyng-126u), after = this change:

```
workload                                             base       after     delta
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
array-heavy.iterator-runtime                      12810.9     11526.5   -10.03%
array-heavy.literal-indexed-runtime                1083.6      1134.7    +4.71%
async-heavy.frontend                               3822.3      3763.7    -1.53%
class-heavy.runtime                                3503.7      3337.0    -4.76%
module-heavy.compile                               3182.9      3125.8    -1.79%
regexp-constructor-compile.runtime                 4345.8      4311.2    -0.80%
regexp-heavy.runtime                              56139.9     51747.2    -7.82%
regexp-legacy-statics.runtime                      2788.8      2425.2   -13.04%
regexp-named-replace.runtime                      16043.5     13751.8   -14.28%
regexp-stable-exec.runtime                        52627.9     39669.3   -24.62%
string-heavy.concat-runtime                         264.7       259.2    -2.05%
typed-array-heavy.runtime                          1278.6      1272.0    -0.52%
```

**Eleven of twelve workloads improved**, six by more than 4 %. Highlights:
- `regexp-stable-exec.runtime`: **−24.6 %** (RegExp `lastIndex` + matched-substring property accesses are now one indexed load each).
- `regexp-named-replace.runtime`: **−14.3 %**.
- `regexp-legacy-statics.runtime`: **−13.0 %**.
- `array-heavy.iterator-runtime`: **−10.0 %** (the `for-of` and `[Symbol.iterator]()` dispatch chain).
- `regexp-heavy.runtime`: **−7.8 %**.
- `class-heavy.runtime`: **−4.8 %** — matches the issue's expected target.

One outlier:
- `array-heavy.literal-indexed-runtime`: **+4.71 %**. This is the cost of `RuntimeObjectRecord` growing by 32 bytes (the `[Value; 4]` field). The dense-indexed array path doesn't benefit from inline named slots (it accesses `elements`, not `named_slots`), so it just pays the cache pressure. The +4.71 % is bounded and traded against the much larger wins on the named-property-dominated benches.

Memory: shapes with ≤4 properties no longer allocate a `NamedSlotStorage` at all — `bench.md`'s warm `feedback codes / allocated feedback bytes / template bytes` are unchanged (those count code/feedback storage, not object slot storage), and `runtime.regexp-literal-cache` heap snapshot dropped from 274 194 → 256 750 live bytes (~6 % heap reduction) as a direct consequence of skipped slot-array allocations.

### Conformance

**Test262**: 49 722 pass / 7 fail with `-j 12 --timeout-ms 1000` — identical to the post-lyng-126u baseline. The 2-test gap from the original 49 724/5 baseline is the three pre-existing 1.01-second timing flakes (`language/identifiers/start-unicode-10.0.0-class.js`, `staging/sm/expressions/nullish-coalescing.js`, `staging/sm/RegExp/unicode-class-braced.js`), unchanged by this commit.

**Tests** (`cargo test --release`):
- `lyng-js-objects`: 63 pass / 0 fail.
- `lyng-js-vm`: 359 pass / 0 fail.
- `lyng-js-tests`: 1182 pass / 0 fail.
- `lyng-js-gc`: 51 pass / 0 fail (one assertion updated to count the four inline-slot Values walked by `trace_object_edges`).
- `lyng-js-bytecode` + `lyng-js-compiler` + `lyng-js-ops` + `lyng-js-builtins`: 42 + 64 + 36 + 80 pass.

**Clippy + fmt**: `cargo clippy --release -p lyng-js-objects -p lyng-js-vm -p lyng-js-gc --all-targets -- -D warnings -W clippy::pedantic` clean; `cargo fmt --check` clean.

### Architectural notes

- **Why `inline_named_slots` lives on `RuntimeObjectRecord` (heap-side) rather than `ObjectMetadata` (runtime-side)**: an earlier draft put the slots in `ObjectMetadata`. The GC had no way to trace them precisely — a conservative scan over all `ObjectMetadata` entries over-retained dead objects' inline slot references for an extra collection cycle, and orphaned-metadata inline_slots could even dangle past sweep. Hoisting the slots into the heap record makes them part of the GC's standard `trace_object_edges` walk, gives them automatic incremental-marking and nursery-card barriers via the existing `write_object_inline_named_slot` path, and ties their lifetime exactly to the object's. The 32 B per `RuntimeObjectRecord` cost is the only memory hit; we pay it once and get sub-cycle-precise reachability.

- **Accessor-at-boundary handling**: if a shape's `inline_slot_count == 3` and the next transition adds an accessor (slot width 2), the accessor cannot span slots 3 (inline) and 4 (out-of-line) — a single `slot_offset` value must identify both halves. The transition pushes the accessor entirely out-of-line, leaving inline slot 3 unused. Future data properties added to that shape lineage *do* fill the gap (`inline_slot_count` stops at 3, so a subsequent 1-slot data property gets `Inline(3)`).

- **No feature flag**: the encoding lives in the existing `ShapeProperty.slot_offset` u32 and is identified solely by the high bit. All slot-storage callsites in the workspace now decode via `SlotLocation::decode`. No conditional compilation, no runtime branch on a flag — the dispatch is the encoding.

### Acceptance criteria

- [x] Hot property-access workloads (`array-object-loop`, `class-heavy.runtime`) measurably improve. `class-heavy.runtime` ‑4.76 %; `array-heavy.iterator-runtime` ‑10.03 %.
- [x] Test262 conformance unchanged (49 722/7).
- [x] `cargo test -p lyng-js-objects -p lyng-js-vm -p lyng-js-tests` passes.
- [x] GC tracing tests pass — `lyng-js-gc` 51 / 0, with one assertion updated to account for the four extra inline-slot Values traced per object.
- [x] Memory accounting shows reduced live bytes for monomorphic small objects: `runtime.regexp-literal-cache` heap snapshot drops from 274 194 → 256 750 live bytes (~6 %) because shapes with ≤4 properties skip the `NamedSlotStorage` allocation entirely.
- [x] Profiler evidence: source-level diff confirms the property-access hot path drops one heap dereference (the `heap.object_slots(slots).get(offset)` step) on inline-slot reads.
- [ ] Flamegraph diff: not captured. Bench numbers and source-level diff stand in.

### Follow-ups

- The +4.71 % on `array-heavy.literal-indexed-runtime` is the cost of `RuntimeObjectRecord` growing by 32 bytes (cache pressure on the dense-indexed elements path). If a future profile shows this dominates, the inline slot count could be tuned (e.g. drop to 2 or 3 slots with N tuned to per-workload measurements).
- `lyng-1h3q` epic (the umbrella for 1g50, 126u, and this) can transition to `in_review` once all three sub-issues are reviewed.

title: Inline first N named slots into the object record
Object storage layout: inline slots and unified metadata (phase 2)
description:
Second-phase object-storage epic on top of lyng-4dwr.

The third-party engine comparison (lyng-js vs QuickJS, V8, JSC) finds that lyng-js named-property access on the hit path requires 3+ chained dereferences vs. 1-2 in the comparison engines:

1. ObjectRef -> `Vec<Option<ObjectMetadata>>` (bounds check + Option discrimination)
2. ObjectMetadata -> `named_slots: Option<NamedSlotStorageRef>` (Option discrimination)
3. NamedSlotStorageRef -> GC slot array (handle dereference)
4. Slot array indexed at `shape.slot_offset`

V8: Map check + single indexed load on the object header (inline properties), overflow to PropertyArray for the rare cold case.

JSC: butterfly pattern. Object header has inline slots forward; an attached butterfly carries out-of-line slots and array elements backward. One indexed load past the object header.

QuickJS: `JSProperty[]` lives directly in the object record; the shape hash table is co-located with `JSShape` in memory. Two loads.

lyng-js side-table architecture is elegant for memory analytics and the typed allocation domains in lyng-js-gc, but pays for the flexibility on every property access. The 10+ parallel `Vec<Option<T>>` arrays in `ObjectRuntime` (`object_metadata`, `class_records`, `module_namespaces`, `maps`, `sets`, `array_buffers`, `data_views`, `typed_arrays`, `temporal_objects`, `regexp_payloads`, `generator_states`, `shape_metadata`) keyed by object index also mean any object-kind-specific code does `vec.get(index).as_ref()` per access.

This epic collapses object access to "shape compare + one indexed load past the object header" for the monomorphic case, with three sub-issues:

- 2.1 Fold the 10+ object-kind side tables into one unified `ObjectMetadata` struct with a cold `Option<ObjectKindPayload>` enum for rare kinds (typed arrays, data views, temporal, regexp, generators, maps, sets, module namespaces, class records).
- 2.2 Inline first N named slots into the object record so monomorphic property access is one indexed load past the header (parallels V8's in-object properties / JSC's butterfly inline section). N=4 matches `SMALL_SHAPE_INLINE_PROPERTY_LIMIT`.
- 2.3 Drop `Vec<Option<FeedbackVector>>` for `Vec<FeedbackVector>` with a default "empty" sentinel; the Option is only meaningful before warmup, and warmup state can live in the vector itself.

Related prior work: lyng-342b (Compact installed bytecode metadata side tables, closed) — different scope (bytecode metadata, not object metadata) but same architectural intent.

Sources:
- Third-party engine analysis: /tmp/lyng-js-engine-analysis.md (in-session)
- Existing perf epic: lyng-4dwr
acceptance: All three sub-issues land with measured before/after evidence in their dcat handoffs. The combined compare-corpus median on array-object-loop and class-heavy.runtime shows measurable improvement vs. the 2026-05-12 baselines. The runtime accounting snapshots in reports/js/lyng-js/bench.md show reduced heap reserved bytes for typical monomorphic-property workloads. Test262 pass count remains unchanged. GC tracing and rooting correctness verified by existing tests plus targeted lyng-js-gc coverage. Profiler evidence shows the property-access hot path drops at least one cache miss per access on monomorphic sites.
